title: Scania's new battery solution enables 720 km range - electrive.com
content:
Commercial Vehicles
Scania is introducing a battery solution for its electric trucks where batteries are mounted behind the cab. In a typical configuration, two MP20 battery packs can be installed behind the cab. This significantly increases battery capacity, enabling ranges of up to 720 kilometers.
New battery technology is being introduced in Scania's electric trucks
Image: Scania
Scania is making it possible to configure battery-electric trucks for greater range without sacrificing the operational flexibility required for European long-haul applications. In a 6×2*4 tractor-trailer combination, additional batteries can be installed behind the cab—alongside the batteries mounted on the chassis.
This offering, called ‘Battery Behind Cab’, works in combination with Scania’s IVD front (Increased Vehicle Dimension). The Swedish manufacturer uses this term to describe a slightly forward-extended, aerodynamically optimised truck front. This new battery arrangement behind the cab is thus possible even when the vehicle’s total length exceeds 16.5 metres.
Scania reduces energy consumption by three per cent
Together with the new front, the vehicle can reduce energy consumption by up to three per cent, depending on equipment and application, as air resistance accounts for a larger share of total energy consumption in electric trucks, according to the company.
“Electric trucks are already part of the transport system, but long-haul operations place very different demands on range, payload and charging. With this solution, Scania is showing how those pieces can come together in a practical way for customers who want to electrify demanding long-distance routes,” says Lars Gustafsson, Senior Vice President and Head of Solutions Management at Scania.
In May, Scania announced that it would offer
seven instead of six battery packs
as a maximum configuration and introduce MCS. These are manufactured by MAN in Nuremberg, with both brands being sister companies within the Traton Group. Now, the topic is becoming more concrete, and Scania states that the new maximum configuration achieves a range of 720 kilometres.
A figure we also know from MAN: at IAA Transportation, the manufacturer announced that its
electric flagship eTGX
as a tractor unit will also be offered with seven battery packs in the future – with a range of the aforementioned 720 km.

title: MCM Intelli-X: Maximum measurement performance with minimal installation space - SMART TESTSOLUTIONS - Batteries News
content:
MCM Intelli-X: Maximum measurement performance with minimal installation space – SMART TESTSOLUTIONS
The MCM Intelli-X measurement and simulation modules are characterised by high channel density, 16-bit resolution, galvanic isolation and a wide-range power supply, all within a minimal footprint.
With the MCM Intelli-X product family, SMART TESTSOLUTIONS presents a new generation of highly precise, compact measurement and simulation modules for use in laboratories, test benches and mobile test systems. The particular advantage of this product family lies in its exceptionally high integration density: Within a very compact footprint, the modules combine multiple measurement or simulation channels, high-resolution 16-bit measurement technology, galvanically isolated channels and a wide-range power supply from 6 to 32 volts. MCM Intelli-X thus offers a combination of performance features that is unique in this size class.
Thanks to their compact and robust design, the modules in the MCM Intelli-X family can be positioned in the immediate vicinity of the devices under test. This reduces cabling requirements and improves signal quality. Positioning directly inside the climate chamber is also possible thanks to the optional IP65 protection rating. At the same time, the integrated signal conditioning protects the measurement technology in the event of short circuits.
Galvanically isolated channels despite the miniature design
A key unique selling point of the product family is the individual galvanic isolation of the channels. Whilst users of compact modules often have to compromise on insulation and safety, MCM Intelli-X combines high channel density with galvanic isolation of every single channel. This allows signals at different potentials to be acquired or simulated safely and reproducibly.
Particularly in high-voltage applications, in battery and fuel cell systems, in industrial test benches or in hardware-in-the-loop environments, this provides additional freedom in system architecture whilst simultaneously increasing operational safety.
Flexible use thanks to wide-range power supply
The integrated wide-range power supply from 6 to 32 volts offers additional flexibility. This allows the modules to be used in both stationary test benches and mobile applications without the need for complex adaptations. The flexibility in supply voltage makes MCM Intelli-X particularly attractive for decentralised measurement and simulation tasks in vehicles, on test benches or in portable test systems.
Attractive cost-effectiveness per channel
In addition to its technical features, the product family also offers compelling economic benefits. The high channel density and high degree of integration result in a particularly attractive price per channel. Users thus gain more functionality in a smaller space whilst simultaneously reducing system costs. This advantage is particularly evident with larger numbers of channels and distributed measurement and simulation applications. This is made possible by the consistent integration of measurement and simulation functions into a compact hardware platform.
The MCM Intelli-X family comprises measurement and simulation modules that can be flexibly combined for a wide variety of applications. Areas of application range from multi-channel systems such as battery systems, fuel cells and electrolysers to general test bench, automation and hardware-in-the-loop applications.

title: COnovate Wins $1,25M DOE Contract to Scale US Graphite-Alternative Anode Production - Batteries News
content:
COnovate Wins $1,25M DOE Contract to Scale US Graphite-Alternative Anode Production
Development contract advances domestic eCOphite™ anode production to improve battery performance and strengthen critical-material supply chains
This award is an important step toward qualifying eCOphite material at commercial scale and strengthening a domestic supply battery materials supply chain.”
— Craig Rigby, President and CEO of COnovateMILWAUKEE, WI, UNITED STATES, September 14, 2026 /
/ — COnovate today announced it has been awarded a $1.25M development contract by the U.S. Department of Energy ‘Critical Minerals and Materials Accelerator’ Program. Under the 24-month agreement, COnovate will continue scaling U.S. production of its eCOphite anode material, a high-performance alternative to graphite-based anodes in lithium-ion batteries, to support U.S manufacturing and address operating challenges in battery systems.
Craig Rigby,
President and CEO of COnovate, said:
This award is an important step toward qualifying eCOphite material at commercial scale and strengthening a domestic supply battery materials supply chain,
“By scaling a graphite-alternative anode material that can integrate with existing manufacturing infrastructure, we are helping customers pursue higher-performing battery systems while reducing dependence on mined critical minerals from overseas”.
The eCOphite solution is designed to address a known challenge in lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery systems: the flat voltage curve that can make state-of-charge harder to estimate across much of the usable range. When used as an additive with existing anodes, the eCOphite material provides a durable voltage reference point and enables existing battery management systems to estimate state-of-charge more accurately and manage packs over their operating life. The result is better system visibility, reduced downtime and warranty risk, and lower costs tied to maintenance and augmentation. The eCOphite material can also be produced domestically from renewable feedstocks, does not require mining, and is designed to drop into existing manufacturing infrastructure.
This work is supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (CMEI) under AMMTO Award Number DE-EE0011730.

title: InoBat and Palmer Energy Technology sign agreement to strengthen European battery energy storage solutions - Batteries News
content:
InoBat and Palmer Energy Technology sign agreement to strengthen European battery energy storage solutions
PETL and InoBat to collaborate on supply chain, Battery and Energy management systems and innovative solutions for Europe and beyond
InoBat and PETL will work together to supply energy storage solutions across Europe, leveraging on their presence in the UK and Ireland as well as in Europe and North America.
PETL and InoBat will have a reciprocal agreement for the supply chain to assure solution availability for customer without shortfalls. In 2026, PETL will supply InoBat with BESS units. In 2027, PETL has the option to take from InoBat´s Slovak manufacturing facility when it is commissioned.
PETL will supply its patented Brill Power battery management system (BMS) and energy management system (EMS) for integration into InoBat´s BESSMONT units.
PETL writes the Brill Power software in Oxford and stores all system data on its own servers in Europe.
Oxford and Bratislava, 15 September 2026.
Palmer Energy Technology Ltd (PETL) and InoBat AS today signed a collaboration agreement to supply battery energy storage systems (BESS) across Europe. A BESS stores electricity and releases it when a customer or the grid needs it.
The agreement covers three areas. It sets out which markets each company will lead. It provides for the supply of BESS units between the two companies. It gives InoBat access to PETL’s battery management technology.
InoBat will build on its established European presence and planned expansion into North America, PETL will leverage its strong position in UK and Ireland. Both companies will address new markets together.
In 2026, PETL becomes a supplier for InoBat, while from 2027 PETL secures the option to take BESS supply from InoBat through its brand BESSMONT, manufactured in Slovakia. In this way both companies create reciprocal cross supply chain to assure availability with no shortfalls for customers.
PETL acquired Brill Power Ltd in 2025. Brill Power’s patented technology is a battery management system (BMS) and an energy management system (EMS). The BMS controls each cell in a battery and keeps the cells in balance. This extends the working life of the battery and increases its usable capacity. The EMS controls when the battery charges and discharges.
PETL’s team in Oxford writes the software. PETL stores all system data on its own servers in Europe. Customers get a European product with their data held in Europe.
In 2025 InoBat launched an energy solutions business to help close Europe’s shortage of grid-scale batteries. Through its BESSMONT platform it has delivered or contracted 875MWh of utility-scale battery energy storage capacity with a strong pipeline increasingly aimed at data center and AI power. InoBat is also developing next-generation sodium-ion technology with partners — a geopolitically resilient chemistry that complements lithium-ion.
Marián Boček,
Co-founder and Chief Executive of InoBat, said:
InoBat strongly believes in partnerships, that enable growth and stability of the business.
”European customers need stable western based BESS supply chain with cyber security and high level quality of product and services. Partnership between PETL and InoBat builds a strong foundation to address energy challenges and prepare Europe for AI-driven future.”
Dr Andy Palmer CMG,
CEO and Co-Founder of Palmer Energy Technology, said:
This agreement gives both companies access to more of the European market.
”PETL brings patented battery management technology and BESS units that are available now. InoBat brings a strong position in Europe and North America and new manufacturing capacity from 2027. Customers in Europe get a European product with their data stored in Europe.”

title: Egypt - PM witnesses signing of contract to build plant for electric batteries CATL - Batteries News
content:
Egypt – PM witnesses signing of contract to build plant for electric batteries CATL
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly on Sunday, September 13, 2026, witnessed the signing of a contract to establish a plant producing various types of electric batteries within the frame of a partnership between Egyptian battery maker BME and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer.
The contract was signed by Chairman of BME Maged Wahib and Luo Director of international investment at CATL Luo Haining, in the presence of Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem, MBA/PMP – Sr. IT Project Manager Amin Karim Ghabbour and BME board member Lotfy Tadros.
BME was established by Egyptian transport manufacturer MCV and Auto D for Industry, Trade and Supplies.
The new plant aims to establish a specialized industrial base for battery systems in Egypt, initially producing batteries for heavy commercial vehicles, with plans to expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.
The project is intended to serve the growing transport and energy sectors and support manufacturing and exports.
The plant’s first phase will have an annual production capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour, with initial investments exceeding 2 billion Egyptian pounds (dlrs 39 million). The second phase will raise capacity to 5 gigawatt-hours annually and include production of passenger-car batteries as well as batteries for storing solar and wind energy.
The project targets a local component ratio of 40% and is expected to supply both domestic and international markets, while creating jobs and developing technical skills for Egypt’s workforce.
The partnership combines Egyptian manufacturing and engineering capabilities with CATL’s battery technology, production equipment and technical support. The plant will supply locally manufactured battery systems to vehicle manufacturers in Egypt, reducing reliance on imports and associated shipping and logistics costs.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Madbouly welcomed the agreement with CATL, saying the company was one of the leading global players in the battery industry and had extensive expertise and capabilities.
He said the government expected work on the project to begin quickly and that it would take the necessary steps to support the development and localization of battery manufacturing in Egypt.
The minister of Industry said the plant represented an important step towards developing Egypt’s domestic battery manufacturing capacity as the global shift towards electric vehicles and energy-storage solutions accelerates.
Hashem said automotive component industries were a cornerstone of Egypt’s national program to develop the automotive industry and were key to attracting global carmakers.
He also said the agreement with the world’s largest electric battery manufacturer demonstrated the ability of Egypt’s industrial sector to meet international manufacturing requirements and produce competitive, high-quality products.
Project manager Amin Karim Ghabbour said the agreement was part of government efforts to deepen local manufacturing, localize modern industries and technologies and strengthen Egypt’s capabilities in producing automotive components, especially for electric vehicles and battery systems.
He said the partnership with CATL would combine advanced global battery technology with Egyptian industrial and engineering capabilities, supporting technology and knowledge transfer and the development of a local supply chain.
Ghabbour further added that BME aimed not only to produce battery systems for heavy commercial vehicles, but also to establish the foundations for an integrated battery industry that could eventually expand into passenger-car batteries and energy-storage solutions.
The expansion, he said, would create new opportunities for investment, manufacturing and exports and support Egypt’s efforts to become a regional hub for emerging industries.

title: R3 Lithium Announces Initiation of Operations to Recover, Refine and Return Critical Minerals to the US Battery Supply Chain - Batteries News
content:
R3 Lithium Announces Initiation of Operations to Recover, Refine and Return Critical Minerals to the US Battery Supply Chain
COVINGTON, Ga. — September 10, 2026 —
R3 Lithium
today announced initiation of operations to produce lithium carbonate from 100% recycled battery materials at North America’s first proven commercial-scale lithium carbonate recovery facility in Covington, Georgia. The company, which also announced that it has secured $15M in Series A funding, from investors including Integral GlobalTech Partners, TDK Ventures and Axial Partners, acquired the 154,000-square-foot facility in July 2026 and retained the leadership team that first demonstrated commercial-scale recycled lithium production at the site in 2025. R3 Lithium holds approximately $1 billion in signed offtake agreements and is investing to bring the plant to continuous commercial operation.
The new funding will be used to upgrade the existing lithium carbonate production line, which was the first in US History to produce 99% purity lithium carbonate from 100% recycled content at production scale. The company projects that the Covington facility will account for more than 50% of the US total production of lithium carbonate in 2027.
R3 Lithium will recover, refine, and return lithium carbonate to the domestic battery supply chain through a calciner-based crystallization and water-based precipitation process that extracts lithium directly from recycled black mass on a single site, without primary mining or non-domestic refining. The plant provides 30,000 metric tons of shredding capacity and a 2,500-metric-ton lithium carbonate production line, with space allocated for an additional 2,500-metric-ton line.
Linh Austin,
President and CEO of R3 Lithium, said:
The U.S. has spent years discussing critical mineral independence while the vast majority of lithium processing has remained overseas,
“R3 Lithium is here today, with a proven facility that has already produced the product, the team that made it happen, and the capital needed to upgrade the line and keep it running, at commercial scale. R3 Lithium is setting a new pace for domestic lithium production, starting now.”
The need for lithium carbonate is widespread and growing, with increasing demand from the defense sector, EV manufacturers, consumer electronics companies, data center operators and other segments. Global battery storage demand rose 51% in 2025, past 300 gigawatt-hours of installations, as data center construction accelerated¹, and global battery energy storage capacity is projected to expand sixfold between 2025 and 2030 at a 42% CAGR². Every gigawatt-hour of grid-scale battery storage consumes approximately 880 tons of lithium carbonate³.
R3 Lithium has secured approximately $1 billion in offtake contracts from customers including Trafigura. “Battery manufacturers, the Department of Energy, and OEMs are increasingly seeking reliable sources of domestic lithium to support the growing U.S. battery supply chain and improve security of supply. To date, however, domestic supply has remained relatively limited,” said Tim Wood-Dow, Battery Metals Trader at Trafigura. “R3 Lithium’s Covington facility helps address that gap in the physical supply chain by producing lithium carbonate from recycled feedstock on U.S. soil.”
A Parallel Pathway to Domestic Lithium Supply
The United States imports most of its lithium, with between 85 and 95 percent of battery cell and component production capacity currently occurring outside U.S. and European borders⁴. Federal policy, including the Inflation Reduction Act and critical mineral designations, is directing substantial resources toward closing that gap, but the timeline for primary extraction remains measured in years, not months. New domestic lithium mines can take seven to ten years to be permitted and more than 20 years from first discovery to first production⁵.
R3 Lithium operates on a different timeline. The Covington facility will produce lithium carbonate from batteries already in circulation, without new mining or foreign refining. A previous owner built the site with approximately $150 million investment; R3 acquired it with no liabilities, fundamentally resetting the economics of domestic lithium production.
R3 Lithium’s growth plan calls for a network of lithium carbonate and black mass shredding facilities across North America and Europe, each engineered in modular 5,000-metric-ton-per-annum units and deployed only with underpinning offtake agreements in place. This approach enables phased capital allocation, early revenue, and repeatable deployment across sites without concentrating risk in a single buildout.
Most battery recyclers split their operations across multiple facilities or geographies. R3 Lithium’s Covington plant processes battery materials from shredding through finished lithium carbonate production in one location. The facility’s shredding lines will produce black mass from both manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries. Lithium is then extracted on-site through R3’s calciner-based process, and the remaining concentrated metal oxide (CMO), rich in nickel, cobalt, manganese, and graphite, is sold separately, often at or above the original purchase price of the input feedstock.
This vertically integrated model gives R3 Lithium multiple revenue streams from a single feedstock and positions the company to supply both lithium carbonate buyers and downstream cathode material producers.
Experienced Leadership, Proven Technology
R3 Lithium’s leadership team combines deep battery materials expertise with large-scale industrial operating experience. CEO Linh Austin brings more than 30 years of experience directing U.S. and international energy businesses, including senior roles at McDermott International, BP, and ARCO. CTO Eric Gratz, Ph.D., who also co-founded Ascend Elements, is the inventor of 43 patents in battery materials and lithium-ion recycling technology and a member of the Technology Committee of the U.S. Department of Energy’s Li-Bridge public-private partnership.
Every battery already in service in this country is a lithium deposit
“It is above ground, it is concentrated, and nobody has to dig for it. What has been missing is the ability to get lithium back out of it, at commercial scale, in the United States. That is the thing we have now demonstrated — not in a laboratory, and not as a pilot.”

title: Battery Research: Distribution of Lithium Isotopes Serves as a Fingerprint for Aging Processes - Batteries News
content:
Battery Research: Distribution of Lithium Isotopes Serves as a Fingerprint for Aging Processes
The service life of lithium-ion batteries is limited by complex aging processes, the causes of which are often difficult to distinguish from one another. Researchers at the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM) have now shown that the distribution of two lithium isotopes within the cells acts like a fingerprint directly linked to the degradation processes. This correlation opens new possibilities for better understanding aging mechanisms and optimizing batteries in a more targeted manner.
Lithium-ion batteries are a key technology for the energy transition. Despite continuous advances in performance and service life, however, one central problem remains unsolved: cells age with every charge and discharge cycle. Their capacity decreases and their performance declines.
Several complex processes inside the battery are responsible for this. To date, the challenge of clearly identifying these aging mechanisms and distinguishing them from one another remains unresolved. While conventional diagnostic methods show that a battery is aging, they often provide only limited information about when, where, and by what mechanism degradation is triggered.
A BAM team led by Carlos Abad and Beatrice Battistella has developed a new approach, which was published in the journal ACS Energy Letters. The researchers use the distribution of two lithium isotopes within a cell as a diagnostic tool for aging processes. Their characteristic traces and patterns provide a fingerprint of the underlying degradation mechanisms.
The method takes advantage of the fact that natural lithium consists of two isotopes: lithium-6 and the slightly heavier lithium-7. These are variants of the same chemical element with different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei. In new batteries, the two lithium isotopes occur in the same proportions as in natural deposits of the alkali metal, namely 2.4% lithium-6 and 97.6% lithium-7.
The researchers investigated lithium-ion batteries with a lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC) cathode and a graphite anode. Measurements on these systems showed that, after the first few charging cycles, lithium-6 began to accumulate preferentially at the anode. Following another 280 cycles, this effect intensified, while the cathode exhibited significantly higher levels of lithium-7. At the same time, the cells’ capacity decreased.
This discovery was made possible by a high-resolution form of mass spectrometry that allowed researchers to determine the distribution of lithium isotopes layer by layer across the entire depth of the electrodes. The research was conducted in collaboration with Nu Instruments Ltd. in the United Kingdom and the Leibniz Institute for Solid State and Materials Research Dresden (IFW Dresden).
Beatrice Battistella
The distribution of lithium isotopes thus provides direct information about aging processes in lithium-ion batteries.
”The isotopes act as natural markers. Their distribution provides insight into the mechanisms that controls lithium movement during battery operation and where changes occur. The researchers were also able to demonstrate that these traces are closely linked to the batteries’ capacity loss.”
For Beatrice Battistella and Carlos Abad, the significance of the results lies primarily in their potential applications for precise measurements: instead of detecting aging solely based on capacity loss, it could be tracked much earlier in the future using the traces left by lithium isotopes in the battery cell. This enables a more precise understanding of aging mechanisms and is ultimately crucial for improving batteries in a more targeted manner and predicting their service life more accurately.

title: Global Battery Materials Signs LOI with LiBEST to Advance Ex-China Graphite and Anode Material Supply - Batteries News
content:
Global Battery Materials Signs LOI with LiBEST to Advance Ex-China Graphite and Anode Material Supply
TORONTO, Sept. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Global Battery Materials Corp. (“GBM” or “the Company”) has signed a non-binding Letter of Intent (“LOI”) with LiBEST, a South Korean battery technology and manufacturing company, regarding the evaluation and potential commercial supply of natural graphite, coated spherical purified graphite (“CSPG”), and other anode materials sourced and processed entirely outside China.
The materials are intended for high-growth applications, including energy, defence, AI infrastructure, and electric vehicles. The LOI establishes a framework for evaluating materials, potential commercial supply, and related development activities, and supports efforts to build a more resilient battery supply chain insulated from geopolitical disruption. The collaboration may also support qualification pathways for GBM’s anode materials across allied-government and defence-related supply chains.
The LOI builds on a prior Memorandum of Understanding between the two companies, which established a framework for collaboration on battery materials testing, anode product development, supply chain engagement, and participation in government programs. Under this framework, LiBEST will evaluate GBM’s graphite and anode materials to strengthen its ex-China supply chain and address applicable U.S. Foreign Entity of Concern (“FEOC”) requirements.
Eric Miller,
Chief Executive Officer of GBM, said:
LiBEST is a frontier battery technology company with a proven ability to design and mass-produce high-performance batteries. They are an ideal partner as we scale our graphite anode materials business
“GBM continues to invest in our anode pilot plant and in developing new product and process IP in Korea. Since launching at the beginning of this year, we have moved quickly to qualify our product with customers urgently seeking a reliable anode supply outside China. In partnership with LiBEST, we are well positioned to meet the lithium-ion battery industry’s exacting standards.”

The close proximity of LiBEST and GBM’s R&D and pilot operations in South Korea is expected to streamline technical communication and accelerate material evaluation and development for both companies.
GBM’s supply strategy is underpinned by its growing mine-to-market platform. The Company is advancing the restart of the Kearney Mine in Ontario as part of a vertically integrated platform spanning critical mineral mining and anode materials processing. The initiative follows two recent Kearney Mine milestones: a positive Preliminary Economic Assessment and a Letter of Agreement with five First Nations supporting responsible development, including potential equity investment.

(TSXV: ETL) (FSE: OW3) (OTCQX: EEMMF), “E3”, “E3 Lithium” or the “Company,” a leader in Canadian lithium development, has entered into a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (the “MOU”) with Epsilon CAM Pvt. title: Dry coating: one technology, many parameters, and one need for tailored current collectors - Batteries News

Dry coating: one technology, many parameters, and one need for tailored current collectors
As dry electrode manufacturing gains momentum across the battery industry, ARMOR BATTERY FILMS highlights
a key challenge often overlooked: each dry
coating process has distinct requirements, making tailored carbon coated
current collectors a critical enabler of industrialization.
Dry electrode coating is one of the most promising innovations in lithium-ion battery manufacturing. By eliminating solvents from electrode production, it offers major economic and environmental benefits, including lower energy consumption, reduced CO₂ emissions, a smaller equipment footprint, and lower operating costs. Despite its potential, dry electrode coating still presents significant technical challenges. Among them, achieving strong and durable adhesion between the electrode and the current collector under competitive conditions, such as process speed and scrap rate, remains critical without the liquid phase used in conventional wet processes.
At ARMOR BATTERY FILMS, our more than 20 years of expertise in the carbon-coated current collector/electrode interface enables us to understand the key parameters that influence dry process performance.
One important lesson stands out: there is no single dry process.
THERE IS
The term dry coating is often used, in contrast to wet coating, as if it referred to a single manufacturing method. In reality, the market is developing a variety of techniques, each with its own parameters and requirements.
Some processes rely on fibrillating binders, while others use spray deposition, powder-based coating, lamination, extrusion, electrostatic deposition, or other innovative approaches. Each technology introduces different constraints in terms of pressure, temperature, electrode composition, physicochemistry, surface energy, and mechanical stress.
As a result, no single carbon-coated current collector can meet all process conditions.
CUSTOM COATINGS TURN CHALLENGES INTO SOLUTIONS
To address this challenge, ARMOR BATTERY FILMS has developed a portfolio of primer technologies that can be adapted to the specific needs of each manufacturing route. Working closely with battery manufacturers, material suppliers, and equipment developers, we have gained direct knowledge of the diversity of dry coating technologies and their specific constraints. This understanding enables us to design tailored solutions that optimize adhesion, improve process robustness, and help unlock the full potential of dry electrode production.
“ARMOR BATTERY FILMS’ coated current collectors have demonstrated strong compatibility with our Kynar® PVDF binders, both in calendaring-based and spray deposition processes.”
Clément Paul
– ARKEMA dry process expert
Today, ARMOR BATTERY FILMS collaborates with leading innovators in the dry process ecosystem, including Arkema, Blue Solutions, Anaphite, InteCell, Fraunhofer IWS, and SFA Nexel, helping accelerate the industrialization of next-generation battery manufacturing.
The future of dry coating will not rely on a single solution. It will rely on dedicated, adaptable solutions. And that
is precisely where ARMOR BATTERY
FILMS brings value.

content:

The PROSPECT Planning Prize supports academic institutions in training skilled professionals to strengthen critical minerals and energy innovation.
September 15, 2026
3 Min Read
The US critical minerals industry needs more skilled workers.
Courtesy of Bet_Noire/iStock / Getty Images Plus
The US Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation (
) has launched the
PROSPECT Planning Prize
, a $16 million initiative to address the critical shortage of skilled professionals in mining and minerals. This prize, part of the broader $100 million Providing Opportunities for Specialized Education in Critical Technologies (PROSPECT) program, seeks to empower academic institutions to develop innovative training programs that will prepare the workforce needed to secure America’s energy future.
Addressing workforce shortages in critical minerals
The initiative comes at a pivotal moment as the US works to rebuild its
domestic battery supply chain
. New mines, processing facilities, manufacturing capacity, and recycling infrastructure are essential to achieving energy independence. However, these efforts require a new generation of engineers, scientists, technicians, and skilled professionals to sustain them.
Related:
Trump's Orders Secure Bulk Power System, Critical Minerals
The PROSPECT Planning Prize encourages academic institutions to design programs that target a diverse range of beneficiaries, including early-career professionals, educators, students in universities, community colleges, and high schools. By expanding access to training and experiential learning opportunities, the initiative helps grow and strengthen the future of the domestic critical minerals industry.
Closing skills gaps in US battery manufacturing
The DOE has launched other efforts, such as the
Battery Workforce Initiative (BWI)
in 2022, yet recruiting skilled labor remains challenging. One of the most urgent challenges the PROSPECT Planning Prize seeks to address is the skills gap in US manufacturing. “Mining and critical minerals professionals are essential to America’s success in manufacturing, AI, energy, and national security—but this country isn't producing enough of them,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “Through this prize competition, DOE will empower universities to pursue more ambitious strategies to attract and educate the workers we need for a robust critical mineral supply chain.”
PROSPECT Planning Prize will reward implementation-ready plans that expand access to training, upskilling, and experiential learning opportunities. AI illustration generated for Battery Technology.
Batteries, particularly lithium-ion batteries, are critical for electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy storage. However, the US domestic workforce lacks the specialized expertise required to support the full lifecycle of battery production—from mining raw materials to recycling used components.
The shortage of skilled professionals in battery manufacturing has slowed down the US’s ability to compete globally in this sector. By investing in
workforce development
, the DOE aims to close these gaps. “This prize is about more than just education—it’s about securing America’s future,” Robertson emphasized. “By building a skilled workforce, we’re not only strengthening our domestic supply chains but also ensuring that the US remains a global leader in energy innovation and manufacturing.”
Related:
Why AI and Critical Materials Are Driving the Future of Battery Supply Chains
$16 Million to transform US workforce development
The PROSPECT Planning Prize challenges US-based academic institutions to submit plans for programs to substantially increase the number of graduates and credentialed professionals in mining and supply chain fields by 2028. Up to 16 institutions will receive $1 million each to implement their plans, focusing on creating pathways to job placement upon graduation or program completion.
Applications for the PROSPECT Planning Prize are now open, with a submission deadline of October 5, 2026. The winners will be announced on October 20. Interested institutions can find more information, including eligibility requirements and submission guidelines, on the
PROSPECT Prize

title: Novartis: Driving Innovative Supply Chains With RLT
content:
Novartis: Driving Innovative Supply Chains With RLT
Prioritise Us
on Google
Steffen Lang, President of Operations at Novartis at Supply Chain LIVE
Steffen Lang, President of Operations at Novartis, took to the Supply Chain stage to explore the technology and operations behind Novartis' healthcare
Steffen Lang, President of Operations
at Novartis, spoke at Supply Chain LIVE about the company's approach to delivering radioligand therapies. The treatment window for these medicines is 72 hours from request to patient delivery, creating one of the most demanding logistics challenges in modern healthcare.
Novartis has built its operations around this time constraint. Each radioligand therapy dose is manufactured for one patient at a specific application time. The company must coordinate manufacturing, handling and transportation of radioactive materials across more than 30 countries and 700 hospitals, ensuring that every dose reaches its destination whilst maintaining the radioactive integrity required for effective treatment.
According to Steffen, the therapy represents a departure from traditional pharmaceutical supply chains. He says: "The company has been pioneering over the past decade, scaling for the first time gene therapies, which provide new hopes for babies and small children."
"And radioligand therapy is another chapter we have just added to it. And bringing those therapies defines reimagine medicine, but also reimagine the way we manufacture," he says.
The shift towards personalised medicine has required Novartis to fundamentally rethink its approach to
pharmaceutical manufacturing
and distribution. Unlike traditional medicines that can be produced in bulk, stored in warehouses and distributed through established pharmacy networks, radioligand therapies (RLT) demand a just-in-time model that leaves no room for delays or errors.
Time-critical logistics network
The 72-hour delivery window creates supply chain requirements that differ from standard pharmaceutical distribution. Novartis tracks each dose using GPS technology and operates a control tower that monitors shipments around the clock, providing real-time visibility across the entire network.
The company follows thousands of doses in transit at any time. Steffen says the contingency planning "involves traffic, air traffic, surveillance and more". This level of monitoring allows Novartis to identify potential disruptions before they impact patient care and implement alternative routing strategies when necessary.
This approach was tested during
severe weather
in the US when 12,000 flights were cancelled, creating widespread disruption across the country's transportation infrastructure. According to Steffen, Novartis reached more than 98% of patients during the disruption, demonstrating the resilience of the company's logistics network even under extreme conditions.
Over the past 12 months, more than 99% of patients have been treated on time, he says. This performance metric reflects not only the robustness of Novartis's systems but also the dedication of teams working across multiple time zones to ensure that no patient misses their treatment window.
The control tower operates as the central nervous system of the entire operation, with specialists monitoring weather patterns, traffic conditions, flight schedules and regulatory requirements across dozens of countries simultaneously. When disruptions occur, the team can rapidly assess alternatives and redirect shipments to ensure on-time delivery.
Steffen Lang, President of Operations
Radioactive material handling
The radioactive nature of RLT adds complexity to manufacturing and transport operations. Steffen explains: "We need to control that as well during that manufacturing supply chain." The radioactive isotopes used in these therapies have short half-lives, which means they decay over time and lose their therapeutic effectiveness if not administered within the designated window.
The company has redesigned production environments and logistics processes to meet regulatory requirements for radioactive products. Each country in Europe maintains different regulations for shipping these materials, creating a complex web of compliance requirements that Novartis must navigate for every cross-border shipment.
"Producing these doses in Italy to ship them or to drive them to Spain is not so easy because regulations regarding shipping radioactive products are very different and regulated in Europe, country by country," Steffen says. This regulatory fragmentation requires Novartis to maintain expertise in multiple jurisdictions and adapt its processes to meet varying standards.
Novartis builds redundancy into its network to address manufacturing or transportation delays. "We look at how to ensure that, if something is delayed, we can pick up the dose from another manufacturing line," Steffen says. This redundancy strategy ensures that a problem at one facility does not prevent a patient from receiving
treatment
The handling protocols extend beyond transportation to include specialised packaging that protects both the product and the people handling it. Each shipment must be clearly labelled, properly shielded and accompanied by documentation that satisfies radiation safety authorities in every jurisdiction through which it passes.
Novartis numbers
72 hours – The window from an RLT request to delivery to the individual patient
99%+ – More than 99% of patients have reportedly been treated on time over the past 12 months
98%+ – Patients reached during a major US snowstorm disruption, despite 12,000 cancelled flights
30+ countries – Novartis is delivering RLT treatments across more than 30 countries
700+ hospitals – The company’s RLT network includes more than 700 hospitals and treatment centres
Automation and tracking systems
Novartis has implemented automation and AI into RLT production over the past 12 to 18 months. The company built a fully automated manufacturing line in Indianapolis that meets radiation safety and aseptic manufacturing standards, reducing human exposure to radioactive materials whilst improving consistency and reliability.
An end-to-end planning and monitoring tool tracks orders from clinical centres through to delivery. The system incorporates mapping and flight-tracking data to identify routes and alternatives when disruption occurs, providing decision-makers with the information they need to respond quickly to changing conditions.
"Beyond advanced therapies, technology and AI is truly changing the way we operate," Steffen says. He says the company's manufacturing network has seen improvements in "quality, reliability of supply, work safety and sustainability and competitive cost" from technology and AI implementation.
The therapy targets cancer cells in focused areas of the body, delivering radiation directly to tumours while minimising damage to surrounding healthy tissue. The individualised approach requires control systems that ensure delivery within the 72-hour window. "The patient has no
treatment
" if the dose arrives outside this timeframe, Steffen says, emphasising the critical nature of every delivery.
The automation systems also provide quality assurance benefits, with built-in checks that verify each dose meets specifications before it leaves the manufacturing facility. This reduces the risk of errors and ensures that patients receive exactly what their clinicians have prescribed.
Steffen Lang, President, Operations at Novartis
Regional manufacturing expansion
Novartis is expanding its manufacturing footprint to position production closer to treatment centres. The company aims to reach 90% of patients within driving distance, according to Steffen, which would significantly reduce the risk associated with air transportation and provide more flexibility in responding to disruptions.
The network now spans more than 30 countries with over 700 hospitals and treatment centres. Novartis is developing its isotope supply network and adding facilities to build redundancy into operations, ensuring that the growing demand for RLT can be met without compromising delivery performance.
For Steffen, the experience shows that supply chain planning cannot be separated from therapy development. "Twenty years ago, manufacturing in parts of certain companies was almost an afterthought," he says, reflecting on how the pharmaceutical industry has evolved in its approach to operations.
"With these therapies, it needs to be built in right from the beginning," he says. Manufacturing, logistics and delivery must be part of the innovation process rather than addressed after therapy development, ensuring that promising treatments can actually reach the patients who need them.
The company's approach treats the
supply chain
as an end-to-end system where orders must be fulfilled within strict parameters. At the end of each order is a patient waiting for treatment, a reality that drives every decision Novartis makes about its RLT operations.

The Digital Supply Chain Award
The Digital Supply Chain Award celebrates the organisations using digital innovation to increase supply chain performance. This can be through the successful integration of automation, or the strategic use of data to deliver better options to clients.
As the world embraces new technology, teams are having to integrate new solutions across the supply chain every day, but knowing which tool to use where is critical. Those considered for the award were demonstrating effective use of innovation to

How does it feel to gain this recognition?
It feels really good. I think the business environment is quite challenging at the moment. Our
sustainability teams
and our sustainability customers are working really hard in quite changing conditions. The market is quite challenging and budgets are being cut, but actually they've been incredibly ambitious and their strategies are delivering real change and we're really proud to be able to say that we've done it together.

title: Kia's new PV7 EV van shows up in the US [Image]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Sep 15 2026 - 8:35 am PT
Shortly after
officially unveiled the PV7, the new electric van was spotted testing in the US.
Is Kia launching the PV7 EV van in the US?
took the covers off the PV7
at IAA Transportation on Monday, the second electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup.
The PV7 is considerably bigger than the PV5, measuring over 17.5 feet (5,350 mm) long, or about 2 feet longer than the PV5 (4,695 mm in length).
Like its first electric van, Kia will offer several PV7 variants, starting with the Passenger and Cargo models.
The PV7 will be available with 71.5 kWh and 96.2 kWh nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery packs. Kia said the Long Range Cargo variant will offer a WLTP range of over 285 miles (460 km).
Front-wheel drive (FWD) will come as standard, but Kia plans to add an all-wheel drive (AWD) variant to the lineup. Depending on the configuration, the FWD powertrain delivers up to 268 horsepower (200 kW) and 309 lb-ft (420 Nm) of torque.
Kia PV7 Cargo (left) and Passenger (right) Source: Kia)
It also uses an 800V electrical architecture, enabling it to charge from 10% to 80% in about 25 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.
The PV7 Cargo (shown below) is designed for delivery, logistics, and other business uses. It’s available in 2- and 3-seat configurations and offers up to 6.1 cubic meters of cargo space. The High Roof variant offers even more, with up to 8 cubic meters.
The Passenger version (shown below), on the other hand, is designed for families or as a shuttle with space for up to nine passengers. In Korea, it will be available as an 11-seater.
Following the Passenger and Cargo models, Kia plans to launch 23 PV7 variants in total. Will the US see any of them?
The same day Kia unveiled the PV7, the electric van was spotted testing in the US. The image from
KindelAuto
shows a disguised prototype during hot-weather testing.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by KindelAuto (@kindelauto)
Kia plans to launch the PV7 in Korea and Europe in the second half of 2027. After that, Kia said “additional markets, derivatives, and conversion models” will follow, but didn’t offer any specifics.
Electrek’s Take
While we are pulling for Kia to bring the electric van to the US, don’t get too excited. The PV5 was caught testing in the US several times, raising speculation that it would eventually go on sale. However, it still hasn’t.
The PV7 could find a market in the US as a larger alternative, but it’s still unlikely that Kia will bring it to the States.
For one, Kia builds the electric vans at a dedicated plant in South Korea, meaning they would be subject to the Trump Administration’s import tax.
Kia’s president and CEO, Ho Sung Song, also told reporters that it chose Hanover, Germany, to reveal the PV7 because it’s aimed at the heart of Europe’s light commercial vehicle segment as a bigger sibling to the PV5.

title: The world's largest EV company just partnered with an African electric motorcycle company
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Sep 15 2026 - 8:15 am PT
Africa’s electric motorcycle market is about to get an interesting new combination of Chinese manufacturing scale and homegrown battery-swapping infrastructure.
Yadea, the Chinese electric two-wheeler giant that has sold more than 100 million vehicles globally, has announced a new strategic partnership with African electric mobility company Spiro. The two companies plan to work together on electric motorcycles and scooters specifically tailored to African markets while integrating those vehicles into Spiro’s rapidly growing battery-swapping network.
And this isn’t exactly a small pilot project.
says it already has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven African countries, supported by over 2,500 battery-swapping stations. The company claims its riders have completed more than 50 million battery swaps and traveled over two billion kilometers.
Now Yadea’s considerable manufacturing muscle is being added to that ecosystem. As the
world’s largest EV company by unit sales
, Yadea knows a thing or two about manufacturing vehicles at scale.
Under the new agreement, Yadea will supply electric two-wheelers and other EV products for Spiro’s markets, while Spiro will integrate those vehicles into its existing swapping and energy infrastructure.
Perhaps more interestingly, the companies say they will jointly develop customized electric two-wheelers designed specifically for African markets. That means adapting the vehicles for local road conditions as well as the heavy commercial use common among motorcycle taxi riders, delivery workers, and other high-mileage operators.
Two-wheelers already serve as essential transportation and commercial tools across much of the African continent. High daily mileage also means the operating-cost savings of switching from gasoline to electricity can add up quickly.
Battery swapping solves another major piece of that puzzle. Instead of asking riders to stop working for hours while charging a motorcycle, depleted batteries can simply be exchanged for charged packs in minutes.
Spiro has been building
that type of infrastructure precisely
, while also expanding regional manufacturing and assembly operations in Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, and Rwanda.
Yadea brings a very different kind of scale to the partnership. Founded in China in 2001, the company says it now operates in more than 100 countries, has 10 production facilities, over 40,000 retail locations, and more than 2,000 patents related to electric vehicle technology.
Spiro, meanwhile, recently raised another $270 million as it works to expand its electric motorcycle and battery-swapping operations.
Put those two pieces together and this partnership could become much more significant than simply another electric motorcycle distribution agreement. Yadea knows how to manufacture electric two-wheelers by the millions, while Spiro has spent years figuring out the considerably harder question of how to actually keep electric motorcycles running all day in African markets.
If the two can successfully combine those strengths, we could be looking at one of the more consequential electric two-wheeler partnerships on the continent yet.

title: NYC’s newest electric school buses come with a money-saving twist
content:
EV Chargers
New York
Electric school buses
Michelle Lewis
| Sep 15 2026 - 8:00 am PT
Photo: First Student
First Student is adding 40 electric school buses in New York City after completing the first phase of a charging project that cut infrastructure costs by 20%.
The electric school buses will serve NYC Public Schools in Brooklyn and Queens, building on a demonstration project with Con Edison that tested a less disruptive way to install charging equipment in a dense urban environment.
At the center of the project is First Charge, First Student’s above-ground charging system. Instead of digging trenches to bury electrical cables, the equipment carries them overhead, cutting construction costs and making installations faster and less disruptive. Here’s how First Charge works:
“Eliminating the need to bury the service line to these chargers lowers the upfront costs for First Student and is a strategy that other fleet owners can replicate to save money and complete projects more quickly,” said Vicki Kuo, senior vice president of Customer Energy Solutions at Con Edison.
That could be especially useful in cities like New York, where digging up paved bus yards can be expensive and complicated.
Con Edison and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) helped fund the demonstration project. The funding included six electric school bus vouchers awarded through NYSERDA’s New York School Bus Incentive Program, plus support for four buses converted from diesel to electric.
The project is also using load-management software to charge buses during off-peak hours, when electricity is generally cheaper. For a large school bus fleet, coordinating charging times can help control energy costs and reduce pressure on the grid.
“Deploying electric school buses at scale requires more than vehicles; it requires the right infrastructure, technology, and utility partnership,” said Kevin Matthews, head of electrification at First Student. “Working with Con Edison, we’ve demonstrated a more efficient approach that can help overcome some of the cost and construction challenges that have traditionally made fleet electrification difficult in dense urban environments.”
First Student is considering more clean-energy upgrades at its Brooklyn facilities, including solar and a smart energy hub.
New York State mandated that all new school buses purchased by 2027 must be zero-emission and all school buses on the road must be zero-emission by 2035.

title: Tesla's record month: 4 fatal Autopilot and Full Self-Driving crashes
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Tesla Full self-Driving
Fred Lambert
| Sep 15 2026 - 7:05 am PT
July 2026 was the worst month on record for Tesla driver-assist crashes. Tesla reported
of them to federal regulators, the most it has ever filed in a single month.
Four of those crashes killed someone. In every one, Tesla’s own data says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, and in every one, the public was never told the system was involved. This is the latest from our
ongoing investigation
matching Tesla’s redacted NHTSA reports to real, named crashes.
A record month, and a rising line
Under a 2021 NHTSA Standing General Order, automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact. Tesla’s monthly count has climbed all year, from 135 in March to 207 in May to 209 in June. July’s 236 is a new high.
Seven deaths, four sealed reports
Each of these appears in Tesla’s July filings, each marked
“Verified Engaged”
— meaning Tesla confirmed through its telematics that the system was on. And on each one, Tesla redacted the three fields that would explain the crash: the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area.
Electrek
, we matched the non-redacted facts about each crash to public reports to better understand each one, since Tesla is trying to limit the information.
Upper Marlboro, Maryland.
Around 12:45 a.m. on July 12, a Tesla Model 3 making a left turn onto Governor’s Park Lane off Route 301 failed to yield to a Harley-Davidson going straight, Maryland State Police said. Three people died: the motorcyclist, Matthew Vowell, 48; his passenger, Krystal Vowell, 47; and a passenger inside the Tesla, Adriana Maxwell, 22. The Tesla was operating as a rideshare. Tesla’s report logs a left turn at 20 mph, driver-assist verified engaged, and says it holds the video. An unprotected left turn across oncoming traffic is a City-Streets maneuver, the kind of thing FSD does and basic Autopilot cannot, the same failure mode as the
Batavia crash we documented
San Mateo, California.
On July 15, a 2016 Tesla Model S left the road, struck a light pole, and caught fire, killing its driver. Tesla’s report: driver-assist verified engaged, 52 mph, a solo strike of a fixed object. It’s a road departure, the single most common crash type in Tesla’s entire driver-assist file.
Ione, California.
Around 7:18 a.m. on July 22, a Tesla heading north on Highway 104 crossed into the southbound lane, sideswiped a Honda, and hit a Cadillac head-on, according to the California Highway Patrol. The Tesla’s driver, Shelby Waldie, 25, was killed; a 2-year-old in the car was hospitalized. Investigators said the reason it crossed the center line is under investigation. Tesla’s report: a brand-new 2026 Model Y, verified engaged, 54 mph. The reason it crossed is the redacted narrative.
Ashby, Minnesota.
Around 3:57 p.m. on July 20, on Interstate 94 in a work zone, a westbound Ford collided with an eastbound Tesla, and a third vehicle then struck them, the Minnesota State Patrol said. Two people died: the Tesla’s driver, Harold Ennulat, 73, and the Ford’s driver, 24. Here, the police made it sound like the Ford was going the wrong way, so the engaged Tesla was likely not to blame. But Tesla’s data still shows the system on at 50 mph, and Tesla holds the EDR and the video.
None of the four was reported publicly as involving Autopilot or FSD. In each, the only reason anyone can connect the death to a driver-assist system is that Tesla had to file a report, which it then redacted.
Tesla’s own count is low
There’s a second problem buried in these filings. Tesla’s report lists a single “highest injury severity.” In Upper Marlboro, three people died, and in Ashby, two did, yet each report records one fatality. Tesla’s federal filings undercount the dead in its driver-assist crashes, which means every aggregate built from this data, including safety comparisons Tesla itself points to, starts low.
Why the redaction matters
Almost no other automaker does this. GM runs a comparable connected-fleet system in Super Cruise and redacts none of its crash narratives. Across the current file, Tesla hides the narrative on 100% of its reports; GM, 0%.
This is the heart of the
investigation
. Tesla is, more than ever, pushing owners to treat a Level 2 driver-assistance system as if it drives itself, selling the software as “Full Self-Driving” while the human stays legally responsible at all times. Then it seals the records that would show how the system behaves when things go wrong, telling regulators it would
“suffer financial harm”
if the public saw them. A motorcyclist, a rideshare passenger, a 25-year-old with her toddler in the car, a 73-year-old man: four people dead in one month, in cars Tesla’s own data says were driving themselves, and not one of those reports says what the car did.
Electrek’s Take
We’ve now matched more than a dozen of these, one by one, from
, and July made the point in a single month: as the crash count climbs to record highs, the fatal cases keep surfacing in Tesla’s data and staying out of the public record. Some of these deaths, like the Minnesota one, may not be Tesla’s fault at all. That’s exactly why the narratives should be open, because right now no one outside Tesla can tell the difference between a crash the system caused and one it didn’t.
We’re careful about the claim. A system being engaged within 30 seconds of a crash doesn’t prove it caused the crash, and the redacted software field means we can’t even separate Autopilot from FSD. But that uncertainty is Tesla’s doing. It has the data, it filed the reports, and it decided that what its cars did in four fatal crashes is a trade secret. Tesla is already
under NHTSA investigation
over how it reports these crashes. Until the narratives open up, we’ll keep matching them.
Even in the Minnesota crash, which I conceded might not sound like Tesla is at fault, the data and crash narrative might still be useful. Maybe the driver was on FSD, not paying attention, and could have avoided or mitigated the crash if they were.

title: Stark turns its 80 hp electric supermoto into a titanium-loaded blacked-out beast
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Sep 15 2026 - 6:33 am PT
Stark Future has already turned its ridiculously powerful electric dirt bike into a street-going supermoto – upon which I recently got to cruise the streets and cities around Barcelona (more on that experience coming soon). But now the company is taking that concept in an even darker direction with the new Stark VARG SM Sköll, a limited-edition, nearly completely blacked-out version of the 80 hp electric supermoto.
And when I say limited, I mean it.
says it will build just 500 numbered examples worldwide, with no second production run planned. And based on
the rate that Stark is selling bikes
, those 500 units aren’t likely to stick around very long.
The name comes from Norse mythology, where Sköll is the wolf that hunts the sun across the sky, eventually destined to catch and devour it. That explains both the name and the rather extreme commitment to blacking out seemingly everything Stark could get its hands on.
Based on the existing VARG SM, the Sköll gets Stark’s full ALPHA specification with 80 hp of peak power as well as tunable Dynamic Traction Control. The underlying bike remains largely unchanged, including the structural 7.2 kWh battery pack, single-speed drivetrain, chassis architecture, and carbon-fiber-sleeved motor with integrated inverter.
But Stark didn’t simply spray a VARG SM black and call it a day. That blackout comes from manufacturing changes, not black airbrushing.
The company says essentially every eligible component received some form of black treatment through anodizing, powder coating, or other finishing processes. That includes the upper and lower triple clamps, steering stem, swingarm, motor housing, inverter casing, charging port cap, docking station, and even the handlebar map switch.
The black anodized triple clamps also receive individual limited-edition engraving.
There is one conspicuous exception to all that darkness: the 520 RK MXU chain retains its gold finish, contrasting against a black 7075 T6 rear sprocket.
Stark also put the Sköll on a bit of a diet.
New 3D-printed titanium footpegs save 140 grams compared to the standard parts, while a complete titanium bolt kit cuts another 900 grams. Together, that trims 1.1 kg (2.4 lb) from the bike, bringing the claimed weight down from 124.5 kg (274.5 lb) for the standard VARG SM to 123.4 kg (272 lb).
That makes the Sköll the lightest VARG SM Stark has produced.
Admittedly, replacing nearly a kilogram’s worth of bolts with titanium probably sits pretty high on the diminishing-returns end of the weight-saving spectrum. But after personally seeing the collection of room-sized titanium 3D printers at Stark’s production facility recently, that’s also exactly the sort of unnecessary excess I’d expect from their 500-unit special edition of an 80 hp electric supermoto.
And considering the VARG platform’s already absurd power-to-weight ratio, shaving off another couple of pounds certainly isn’t going to hurt. The crazy experience is only going to get a bit crazier.
The Stark VARG SM Sköll’ 500 units will start with their first deliveries scheduled for October 2026.
For anyone who looked at the regular VARG SM and thought, “This is great, but it needs more titanium and less color,” it looks like your motorcycle has just arrived.

title: This Brooklyn startup will put nearly 700 EV plugs on NYC curbs
content:
EV Charging
New York
Curbside Charging
Michelle Lewis
| Sep 15 2026 - 6:10 am PT
Photo: it's electric
New York City has chosen Brooklyn-based
it’s electric
to supply the hardware for its permanent curbside EV charging network, which will bring nearly 700 Level 2 charging points to all five boroughs over the next three years.
The rollout will replace the city’s existing pilot infrastructure and add 600 new charging points to the current 88. The chargers will be manufactured in Queens.
NYC DOT announced the expansion
in early August
but didn’t reveal who would supply the chargers. The agency is working with the New York Power Authority on procurement and installation.
Each PlugNYC station will have at least two charger posts with two plugs each, for a minimum of four charging points per site. Engineering and construction will be handled by Maverick Corporation, and SWTCH Energy will provide the software platform.
The stations are deliberately headed for dense neighborhoods where residents rely on street parking – especially communities with large numbers of Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) and rideshare drivers. Initial locations include Soundview and Unionport in the Bronx; Rego Park, Forest Hills, and Far Rockaway in Queens; Red Hook, Carroll Gardens, and Bedford-Stuyvesant in Brooklyn; the Upper West Side and Washington Heights in Manhattan; and Stapleton on Staten Island.
That location strategy matters because half of New York City’s car owners park on the street. Without a driveway or garage, charging an EV at home isn’t an option.
The city’s existing curbside chargers are already occupied by an EV more than 70% of the time, with utilization approaching 99% at some locations.
Just as fire hydrants are on every street, our vision is for EV chargers to become that normal – infrastructure New York’s kids simply grow up with,” said Nathan King, cofounder and CEO of it’s electric.
The buildout will also support the city’s
Green Rides initiative
, which requires that 100% of Uber and Lyft trips be completed in zero-emission or wheelchair-accessible vehicles by 2030. New York’s rideshare drivers are already completing around 3 million EV trips per month, according to NYC DOT.
Pricing hasn’t been set yet, but NYC DOT will retain control over what drivers pay. Charging will be billed by the kilowatt-hour, and drivers will be able to pay through multiple apps or by tapping a credit card. The city says prices will be structured to remain affordable while encouraging drivers to move their cars when charging is finished.
Where possible, the sites will also include electrical connections for e-bike charging, electrified bike-share docks, secure bike parking, or cargo-bike hubs.
it’s electric launched its first New York curbside charging pilot at the Brooklyn Army Terminal in Sunset Park in 2023 and is headquartered at Newlab in the Brooklyn Navy Yard. It now operates in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Detroit, Washington, DC, and Boston.
The company has also announced a new funding round led by Halogen Ventures, bringing its total funding to $15 million. The company says every charger it supplies as it expands across North America will be built in Queens.

title: Segway’s new 28 MPH MUXI Pro cargo e-bike gets automatic shifting and regen braking
content:
Micah Toll
| Sep 15 2026 - 6:00 am PT
Segway is giving its compact MUXI utility e-bike a fairly significant upgrade, adding everything from automatic electronic shifting to front suspension and a higher Class 3 top speed.
The new Segway MUXI Pro builds on the company’s existing short-tail cargo e-bike platform,
launched earlier this year
as part of Segway’s continued expansion into the electric bike industry.
The design retains the distinctive swooping step-through frame while packing in a number of features that should make it more capable as an
everyday car-replacement-style e-bike.
Perhaps the most interesting upgrade is the new 9-speed electronic drivetrain with automatic shifting.
Besides saving riders from having to think about shifting, the wider drivetrain also helps the MUXI Pro reach a pedal-assisted top speed of 28 mph (45 km/h). Riders can select between Class 1, 2, and 3 operation through the Segway app, subject of course to local regulations.
As such regulations continue to shift and fragment in cities and states around the US in absence of a single federal standard, riders are reminded to check their local laws.
Power comes from a 750W direct-drive rear motor producing 80 Nm of torque, paired with a 716Wh battery. Segway claims up to 73 miles (117 km) of range, though as usual, expect real-world range to vary considerably based on assist level, terrain, rider weight, and riding conditions.
That direct-drive motor also enables regenerative braking and Hill Descent Control (basically like engine braking on an ICE vehicle, where the bike won’t simply continue accelerating due to gravity), while Hill-Start Assist helps prevent the bike from rolling backward on inclines. There’s even traction control designed to detect rear wheelspin.
Another major improvement is the addition of a 70mm front suspension fork, addressing one of the limitations of many rigid utility bikes. Hydraulic disc brakes with 180mm rotors handle stopping duties, while the bike rolls on chunky 20×3-inch tires. Front and rear fenders are now standard equipment, as are turn signals integrated into the lighting system.
Don’t forget thought that this is still very much a utility bike. The MUXI Pro is rated for a hefty 418 lb (190 kg) total payload, and Segway offers an optional passenger kit rated for passengers up to 120 lb (54 kg). Front and center baskets are also available.
Segway has loaded the bike with its increasingly expansive suite of smart features, too, including Apple Find My, GPS tracking, proximity-based AirLock, Lost Mode, OTA updates, and a color TFT display with navigation. Some connected features require a subscription after the first year, as is common for GPS and data-connected services.
At 82.2 lb (37.3 kg), the MUXI Pro certainly isn’t a lightweight e-bike, but that’s not really the point here. It’s a compact cargo bike designed to carry people and stuff without growing into the footprint of a full-size long-tail.

title: Spain added 10.1 GW of solar in 2025 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Spain installed 10.1 GW of new solar capacity in 2025, including 8.97 GW of ground-mounted PV and 1.14 GW of self-consumption systems, according to Spanish PV association UNEF. The trade body says falling captured prices are increasing pressure on new projects and underscoring the need for storage and greater electrification.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
15 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
A PV plant operated by Iberdrola in Spain
Spain’s solar sector installed 10,105 MW of new capacity in 2025, according to the annual report of Spanish PV association UNEF.
Solar accounted for nearly 23% of the country’s electricity mix, making it Spain’s leading power-generation technology. Ground-mounted installations accounted for 8,966 MW of the new capacity, up 31% from 2024. The self-consumption segment added 1,139 MW, down 4% year on year.
UNEF said strong daytime solar generation is lowering wholesale electricity prices while also reducing the revenue earned by PV assets. The average price captured by solar fell from €42.28 ($48.82)/MWh in 2024 to €36.39/MWh in 2025 and €29.68/MWh in the first half of 2026.
The decline coincided with a rise in the number of zero- and negative-price periods. Spain recorded 797 hours with electricity prices at or below €0/MWh during periods of significant PV generation in 2025. The country had already matched that figure by July 7, 2026, and was approaching 900 hours by early September.
UNEF identified the electrification of end uses as one of the main challenges in the next phase of the energy transition. Spain has 71.5 GW of demand connection capacity that has either been granted or included in grid planning through 2030, alongside a further 24 GW of pending requests. Data centers, industrial facilities, hydrogen production, storage and electric mobility account for a significant share of the expected demand.
Storage is also becoming increasingly important. Behind-the-meter storage installations rose 65% in 2025 to 540 MWh, bringing cumulative capacity installed since 2022 to 2,745 MWh.
Spain also has 261 MW of utility-scale storage in operation, comprising 241 MW of hybrid systems and 20 MW of standalone projects. A further 33,031 MW has secured permits, while 14,607 MW remains in the permitting process.
Solar contributed €9.84 billion to Spain’s gross domestic product in 2025, equivalent to about 0.5% of national GDP, while the sector’s total economic impact reached €14.12 billion. The industry supported 134,708 jobs and generated €3.21 billion in exports.
Investment in research, development and innovation reached €473 million. UNEF put the sector’s innovation intensity at 3.6%, more than twice the 1.6% average for Spanish industry.
The association said the next stage of solar development will require the electricity system to accommodate higher volumes of renewable generation and storage. Its proposals include introducing more flexible grid-access and connection permits, streamlining administrative procedures, facilitating the hybridization of existing plants and accelerating demand electrification.
UNEF also called for changes to the wholesale price-setting mechanism to reflect growing renewable penetration, including measures aimed at limiting the frequency of zero-price periods.
