title: Greece clears way for balcony PV systems up to 800 W - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Greece has overhauled its self-consumption rules, permitting plug-in balcony solar systems up to 800 W and standalone batteries for the first time. The framework also simplifies installation procedures, supports storage additions and expands self-consumption opportunities for islands, public entities and residential communities.
Ilias Tsagas
15 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Residential
Greece’s Ministry of Environment and Energy has published a new policy framework overhauling the country’s self-consumption regime. The framework does not require parliamentary approval and took effect immediately.
The ministry said the new framework “makes self-consumption simpler and more flexible, streamlines procedures, and expands opportunities for consumer participation.” It follows
a public consultation that took place in the summer
For the first time in Greece, the framework allows plug-in PV systems of up to 800 W, commonly known as balcony solar, as well as standalone batteries that are not connected to renewable energy systems.
Balcony solar systems and standalone batteries must be used exclusively for self-consumption and cannot inject electricity into the grid. However, when combined with dynamic electricity tariffs, the ministry said these systems will allow consumers “to store energy from the grid during periods of lower prices and utilize it to meet their needs during periods of higher prices, thereby reducing their energy costs.”
Plug-in PV systems must be installed alongside smart meters so the local distribution grid operator can monitor them remotely. They must also comply with specific safety requirements designed to protect the grid and other electrical installations. The grid operator must publish the requirements on its website by Oct. 31, 2026, and installers will be required to sign a document confirming compliance with the specifications.
Although balcony solar systems cannot inject electricity into the grid, the framework allows the grid operator “to identify sections of the grid where connecting new ‘balcony photovoltaics’ is not feasible due to limited capacity to absorb additional generation, and to prohibit their connection in those specific areas,” according to the ministry.
New self-consumption regime
The ministry said the framework will overhaul Greece’s self-consumption market by simplifying the development and operation of such systems. The main policy changes are as follows.
The framework establishes an electronic registry of energy self-consumers containing data on self-consumption systems and electricity supply points. Combined with the installation of smart meters, the registry is expected to improve management of the self-consumption market.
Self-consumption systems on the Greek mainland and islands will be permitted to add batteries, subject to technical requirements.
Some self-consumption systems in Greece have already been installed with batteries
, but the framework will allow batteries to be added to existing systems that do not have them. Batteries installed alongside PV systems on the islands will not be permitted to inject electricity into the grid.
The framework also aims to expand self-consumption on Greece’s islands. The ministry plans to allocate €476 million ($549.5 million) through the
Islands Decarbonization Fund
to support such projects.
The ministry has also clarified the compensation process for self-consumption systems that inject excess electricity into the grid. Surplus electricity supplied to the grid will be compensated at day-ahead market prices.
Systems on non-interconnected islands, which do not supply electricity to the mainland grid and therefore do not participate in the mainland electricity market, will be compensated at a special market price set separately for each renewable energy technology. The prices are periodically set by Greece’s Operator of Renewable Energy Sources and Guarantees of Origin, a state institution.
The policy establishes procedures for settling all self-consumption schemes, including net metering, virtual net metering, net billing and virtual net billing. The ministry said this will simplify relationships among system owners, electricity suppliers and aggregators while accelerating payments.
Special provisions will allow local authorities, public-sector entities governed by public or private law, and charitable foundations to operate self-consumption systems under net-billing and virtual net-billing schemes.
Schools, health centers, hospitals, sports facilities, street-lighting networks, and water and sewage infrastructure will therefore be able to install PV and battery systems and receive credits for the electricity they generate directly on their power bills. Such provisions previously applied only to residential self-consumption systems.
Group self-consumption, previously available to residents of the same building, will be expanded to include consumers within residential complexes, enabling neighborhood-level self-consumption projects.
The Hellenic Association of Photovoltaic Companies (Helapco), one of Greece’s main solar industry associations, welcomed the framework, saying it “incorporates most of the market’s proposals, as well as new regulations mandated by EU directives.”
Helapco said weaknesses in the previous regulatory framework had caused Greece’s self-consumption market to stagnate.

title: The value of solar PV in Northern regions is widely underestimated - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Contrary to conventional perceptions, solar PV can be an important component of a viable Arctic energy system, thanks to the region’s long summer days. Its low cost makes it competitive even in areas with long, dark winters, particularly when other renewable energy sources provide insufficient output.
LUT University
15 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Wind power and solar PV monthly full load hours in Finnish Lapland.
The conventional perception of the Arctic region has been that the long, dark winters render solar PV almost useless, making wind power the go-to solution for energy experts. However,
research on seasonal complementarity in Finland
shows that this perception overlooks a crucial aspect: the flip side of long winters is an equally long summer with long daylight. It is a fact that everyone acknowledges in theory but often disregards in practice.
The highest solar PV yield per installed capacity for a single day has been recorded in
Antarctica
, where the sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours during the summer solstice. The ground reflection because of snow and the cold environment further boost the yield. This phenomenon highlights the potential for solar PV in polar regions.
Exploring the solar PV potential in the Arctic region reveals PV can play a surprisingly significant role. Another study on the
energy transition in Finnish Lapland
shows that gigawatts of solar PV can be crucial during the summer months when wind power is at its lowest. This could aid Lapland in becoming an e-fuels export hub, revolutionizing the region’s energy landscape.
But Lapland is not an isolated case. Research on the potential of
Greenland
, and the
Shetland Islands
to become e-fuel export hubs based on their vast wind resources demonstrates solar PV can contribute meaningfully to the energy balance during the summer months. The study on
Greenland
shows that solar PV contributes over 10% of annual electricity, helping to run e-fuel synthesis units in summer months. Even
, with its abundant geothermal and wind energy, can benefit from the summer boost provided by solar PV. Similar findings are reported for the
entire Nordic-Baltic region
, which will be mostly powered by wind power while solar PV is an indispensable energy resource.
Solar PV performance in the Arctic and sub-Arctic region
A recent publication on
the prospects of solar PV in the Arctic and sub-Arctic region
investigates how different solar PV technology portfolios perform across the Arctic, combining high-resolution modeling with a detailed cost analysis. The findings reveal that horizontal single-axis tracking (HSAT) solar PV systems can deliver between 770 and 2170 full load hours per year, depending on location. Interestingly, simpler designs perform nearly as well. East-west oriented vertical bifacial (EW vertical) solar PV systems typically generate only 0-13% less electricity than HSAT. In some extreme northern locations, they can even match tracking systems. As an example, in Nunat, Greenland (77.4°N 67.9°W) they generate equal annual output.
The study also shows clear economic advantages. Compared to a reference mix of technologies (40% fixed-tilt, 50% HSAT and 10% EW vertical), switching to a fully EW vertical portfolio reduces the levelized cost of electricity by 1.4-14% in high Arctics. Complex tracking is not always necessary to achieve favorable generation patterns in the North. By combining EW vertical with optimally fixed-tilt solar PV systems, it is possible to closely replicate the daily production profile of HSAT. For instance, a 50/50 mix of those two configurations reaches a high correlation with HSAT generation patterns for sub-Arctics.
Levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) for the reference technology portfolio (reference) and relative change in LCOE for fixed-tilt, single-axis tracking (HSAT), and East-West vertical (EW Vert) setups). Image: LUT University.
These findings have important implications for the energy system design. Simpler, non‑tracking PV solutions can ease deployment in remote Arctic regions while maintaining strong performance. Such flexible configurations can support national energy transitions, including emerging
integrated PV
approaches such as agrivoltaics and the electrification of transport corridors. This highlights how well‑designed solar PV portfolios can enable more integrated, resilient, and cost‑effective clean energy pathways in high‑latitude regions. Similar results have been found for
Alaska and the very north of Canada
, where inter-regional grids are less present, and more local micro-grids form the electricity supply of the population.
Especially vertical solar PV should be considered in more detail. Not only is it possible to harvest the midnight sun more effectively, but in
combination with agriculture
, vertical solar PV offers
various side-benefits
. Vertical solar PV can act as a wind shelter, which can be important for sensitive crops, and their electricity generation profile better matches the demand. Furthermore, vertical solar PV systems are less prone to snow cover.
Solar PV is needed in Iceland to support carbon dioxide removal
Another northern region rarely discussed in solar PV conversations is Iceland, the country with the northernmost capital city. Iceland is known for its large aluminium industry powered by hydropower and geothermal energy. Industry opportunities also exist for novel areas, such as carbon dioxide removal (CDR). Research on the
CDR service opportunities of Iceland as a new industry sector
reveals a large potential; however, not without side-effects. The new industry sector would add significant amounts of baseload energy demand, while the sustainable potential of conventional renewables is almost fully utilized.
Fortunately, Iceland is blessed with an abundance of renewable energy sources. The first that comes to mind is wind power. In the North Atlantic, Iceland shows similarly good wind yields as the north of Great Britain or the south of Greenland. Furthermore,
wave power
could play an important role, as Iceland might be one of the few examples where wave power outcompetes
offshore wind power
. Over a wide range of scenarios, solar PV always plays a crucial role.
Even when the energy demand of the CDR sector is considered becoming more flexible to follow the availability of renewable energy sources, solar PV is always needed to cover for the significant seasonality of wind power and wave power. With heat demand even during the summer, solar PV becomes the backbone of a stable energy system year-round.
The value of solar PV for the North
Depending on scenarios the share of solar PV to the annual electricity generation in 2050 can reach up to 7% for
, 9% for
Greenland
, 17% for
, 1% for the
Shetland Islands
, 30% for
, and 33% for the very
North of Canada
. A recent study for the
Nordic-Baltic
region found a solar PV share in electricity generation of 17-22% and 44-54% in installed capacity. A recent
global review study
on the share of solar PV in electricity generation by 2050 finds decent shares around 10-20% across the entire Arctic and sub-Arctic regions in the northern hemisphere.
The answer behind the value of solar PV in regions far from the equator lies in its remarkably low capital and operational expenditures, which are expected to continue declining. Not only utility-scale PV plants but also
prosumer PV
systems are becoming attractive in Arctic regions. In cost minimization studies, solar PV consistently emerges as a key player, even in regions with the longest and darkest winters. This serves as a reminder that even in regions with the lowest solar yield, the reduction in full load hours is only twofold compared to the regions with the highest yield. This means that solar PV can still deliver a significant amount of energy, even in the most challenging conditions.
As the energy landscape continues to evolve, it’s time to rethink the assumptions about solar PV in the Arctic and Northern regions. The research is clear: solar PV is a vital component of a cost-optimized energy system, independent of the location.
Authors: Rasul Satymov, Geethike V. Arachchi, Dominik Keiner, and Christian Breyer
This article is part of a monthly column by LUT University.
Research at
LUT University
encompasses various analyses related to power, heat, transport, industry, desalination, and carbon dioxide removal options. Power-to-X research is a core topic at the university, integrated into the focus areas of Planetary Resources, Business and Society, Digital Revolution, and Energy Transition. Solar energy plays a key role in all research aspects.

title: California cold-storage provider sues solar businesses over $1 billion rooftop fire  - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Cold-storage giant Lineage claims a $1 billion fire at its 46,451.52 m² facility was ignited by an improperly maintained rooftop solar array following ignored safety warnings.
Ryan Kennedy
15 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
An aerial view of the rooftop after the fire burned for eight days.
Cold-storage REIT Lineage, Inc. has filed a civil lawsuit in Los Angeles County Superior Court against commercial solar operator Altus Power, Inc., its project subsidiary Los Palos Street Operating, LLC, and maintenance contractor Pearce Services LLC, alleging operational negligence caused the June 17 fire that destroyed Lineage’s 46,451.52 m² facility in Boyle Heights.
The facility served as a central hub for temperature-controlled logistics, housing tens of millions of pounds of perishable food items including frozen meats, produce, and commercial grocery stock.
The lawsuit seeks more than $1 billion in damages, citing counts of negligence, negligent supervision, breach of contract, and state health and safety code violations.
According to the complaint, the fire originated within the facility’s rooftop solar array, which spans an area equivalent to eight football fields, while crews from Pearce Services were conducting testing and work on the energized system.
Lineage contends that the solar operator and contractor re-energized the array despite explicit, written instructions from Lineage on June 11 to keep the system off until critical safety and voltage checks were performed.
“This lawsuit is about Altus and Pearce starting this fire and then being nowhere to be found when the community needed help,” Lineage President and chief executive officer Greg Lehmkuhl said in a statement. “The record is clear: this was a solar fire. Cold storage is not a risk to communities.”
Industry safety benchmarks cited by UL (Underwriters Laboratories) and the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) place the risk of residential rooftop solar fires in the U.S. at roughly 0.1 fires per 1,000 systems per year, or about 0.01%.
The legal filing reveals a prior safety incident at the site in August 2024, when a smaller fire broke out in the same rooftop array. Following that event, Altus retained Pearce, a subsidiary of real estate brokerage firm CBRE, to reconfigure the system.
However, internal inspection records cited in the complaint indicate that by May 2026, inspectors had identified over 200 PV connector failures across the array, including mismatched jumper connections and loose bolts in the specific quadrant where the June 17 fire began.
The fire burned for eight days, triggering local emergency declarations and leaving nearly 85 million pounds of food inside the destroyed freezer before an intensive, two-month cleanup effort was completed on September 5.
Lineage claims it spent over $100 million on direct site remediation, environmental cleanup, and neighborhood relief efforts, costs it now seeks to recover along with property losses and indemnification against pending class-action suits brought by local residents.
Both Altus Power and Pearce Services have rejected the claims.
A spokesperson for Altus called the lawsuit “riddled with misinformation” and a “blatant attempt to deflect blame for their role in this matter, including any damage caused by the release of substances from the warehouse, not the solar panel.”
Pearce Services stated that drawing early conclusions is premature while official cause-and-origin investigations remain ongoing.
The Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) has not yet issued its final investigative findings regarding the official cause of the blaze.

title: Biwatt releases sodium-ion storage system for C&I applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Biwatt launched the modular PowerLake I3 sodium-ion storage system for C&I applications, offering 43.6 kWh–2.09 MWh configurations using NFPP cells. Available as indoor racks or IP55 outdoor cabinets, it delivers up to 65.5 kW per 130.8 kWh unit and is rated for 8,000 cycles.
Emiliano Bellini
15 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Biwatt PowerLake I3 system
Chinese energy storage system manufacturer
has unveiled a modular sodium-ion battery energy storage system for commercial and industrial (C&I) applications.
The PowerLake I3 platform spans configurations from 43.6 kWh to 2,092.8 kWh and is offered as an indoor rack or an outdoor cabinet. It is built around 8.72 kWh packs using 170 Ah sodium-ion cells with sodium iron phosphate pyrophosphate (NFPP) chemistry.
Five to 15 packs can be assembled into an indoor cluster, corresponding to 43.6 kWh to 130.8 kWh. At system level, the 130.8 kWh rack can be deployed in groups of up to five, while as many as 16 outdoor cabinets can be connected in parallel, according to the company. That puts the respective maximum capacities at 654 kWh and 2,092.8 kWh.
Both 130.8 kWh variants have a rated voltage of 769.5 V, a battery voltage range of 540 V to 918 V and rated power of 65.5 kW. Standard charge current is 85 A, while maximum continuous charge and discharge current is 170 A. Biwatt recommends operating at 90% depth of discharge.
The datasheet lists 8,000 cycles under test conditions of 25 C plus, 0.5 C charging and discharging, and 80% depth of discharge. It does not state an end-of-life capacity threshold for that cycle figure.
The indoor PLR-130-40 rack uses natural convection cooling and carries an IP20 rating. It measures 1,780 mm x 1,210 mm x 920 mm and weighs less than 1.82 tons. Charging is specified from 0 C to 55 C, while discharge is supported from -30 C to 55 C.
The outdoor PLC-130-40 cabinet uses air cooling and has an IP55 enclosure. It measures 1,144 mm x 2,172 mm x 1,446 mm and weighs 2.002 tons. Biwatt specifies both charging and discharging across a temperature range of -30 C to 55 C.
The two formats are rated for operation at up to 4,000 meters altitude and at 5% to 95% relative humidity. For controls and integration, the outdoor cabinet supports RS485, CAN, USB and Ethernet communications, while the rack lists CAN connectivity.
Biwatt says the system is compatible with mainstream inverters and energy management platforms and supports remote maintenance and over-the-air updates via Ethernet.
The manufacturer lists IEC/EN 61000, IEC/EN 62477, UL 1973 at cell level, UL 9540A and UN 38.3 among the applicable standards and test references.
Pricing, warranty terms and commercial availability were not included in the product materials reviewed.

title: PPA prices rise 2.2% in Europe in August - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
European PPA prices rose 2.2% in August, led by a 4.9% increase in the United Kingdom, while announced PPA capacity fell sharply to 335 MW. Corporate buyers dominated PPA activity, as storage-related agreements held steady at 869 MW and included major BESS deals in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
15 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
European power purchase agreement (PPA) prices rose 2.2% in August, according to the Euro Composite Index from Swiss consultancy Pexapark. The United Kingdom recorded the largest monthly increase, at 4.9%, followed by Germany and the Netherlands, both at 2.8%, and Italy, at 1.6%. Prices remained virtually unchanged on the Iberian Peninsula. France posted a marginal increase of 0.2%, while prices in the Nordic markets fell 1.2%.
The increase in the United Kingdom was largely driven by revised PPA benchmark values following an update to Pexapark’s market price risk assessment. The consultancy said market evidence indicates that buyers have reduced the discounts applied to this risk, raising contract values across a range of technologies and structures. The effect was most pronounced for longer-term contracts, with prices for a 10-year PPA rising by around GBP 5 ($6.80)/MWh for comparable start dates.
European PPA activity slowed significantly in August, with 14 agreements covering around 335 MW announced during the month. This compares with 24 agreements totaling approximately 1.1 GW in July. Pexapark said the slowdown was partly attributable to the European summer holiday period.
Corporate buyers accounted for 13 of the 14 agreements and approximately 298 MW, equivalent to 89% of the reported capacity. Onshore wind dominated, with around 214 MW, or 64% of the total, largely due to four agreements signed by Amazon in Sweden. Solar accounted for approximately 89 MW, while the remaining 37 MW came from a hybrid solar-plus-storage PPA in Germany.
Activity involving flexibility purchase agreements (FPAs) increased in August, with 11 deals covering approximately 869 MW and 2.4 GWh of reported storage capacity. The total volume was virtually unchanged from July despite the lower number of transactions.
Merchant revenue-sharing arrangements accounted for four deals totaling 374 MW, including the month’s largest agreement, for the 300 MW Iceni battery energy storage system (BESS) in the United Kingdom. Three tolling agreements added 309 MW, led by a 200 MW contract signed by Vattenfall for the Sirius project in the Netherlands. A 10-year agreement covering an 80 MW project in the United Kingdom, featuring a revenue floor and market participation, was also announced.
In Germany, MaxSolar and DB Energie announced the country’s first time-profiled hybrid PPA, combining a 37 MW solar plant with a 15 MW/30 MWh battery. The agreement enables solar generation to be shifted to different times of day. Meanwhile, the 200 MW tolling agreement for Sirius highlights progress on flexible grid-connection arrangements for large-scale BESS projects in markets facing grid constraint

title: Researchers find strong vendor-to-vendor variation in UVID performance of TOPCon solar cells - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
US researchers found significant manufacturer-dependent differences in UV-induced degradation and light-assisted recovery among commercial TOPCon solar cells. The results highlight the need for controlled light soaking before testing and for accounting for daily dark-degradation and recovery cycles in performance models.
Emiliano Bellini
15 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
A US research team has investigated metastable dark degradation and light recovery in commercial TOPCon solar cells exposed to
ultraviolet-induced degradation
(UVID), finding significant variation among manufacturers.
The scientists said previous studies had identified significant UVID in TOPCon devices, with reported degradation rates comparable to or higher than those observed in earlier commercial technologies such as PERC. However, they noted that light soaking or current injection can reverse some of the resulting damage.
Their technical analysis focused on unencapsulated M10 bifacial TOPCon solar cells supplied by three undisclosed manufacturers, designated Vendor 1, Vendor 2 and Vendor 3.
“All cells are commercially available and intended for module production,” the researchers said, without providing further details about the manufacturers.
The team examined metastable recovery under illumination and subsequent degradation in darkness using localized external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements. It used controlled light soaking from the EQE system’s lamp to determine how exposure dose and wavelength affect recovery. The researchers then compared recovery trends among the three vendors to assess variations between commercial cells with nominally identical structures.
The analysis showed that differences in materials and manufacturing caused vendor-specific degradation responses, despite the cells sharing the same nominal architecture. Variations in layer thickness, composition, compositional gradients and microstructure may have little effect on initial performance but become pronounced during long-term UV exposure, the researchers said.
UV exposure produced clear differences among the manufacturers. Cells from Vendors 2 and 3 lost about 4% of their short-circuit current density, while those from Vendor 1 lost less than 1%. UV-range quantum efficiency losses reached approximately 40% for Vendor 2, compared with about 10% for Vendors 1 and 3.
The assessment also showed that UV light could partially restore performance following accelerated UV aging and dark storage. Recovery was strongest at wavelengths between 320 nm and 340 nm and generally occurred within seconds under sunlight or suitable UV illumination.
Light soaking produced the strongest recovery in cells with the greatest UV-induced degradation, making the procedure essential for accurate measurements. Although the extent of recovery varied among vendors, the required exposure dose was similar. The cells typically returned to a dark-degraded state within approximately 55 hours, suggesting that they could degrade overnight and recover rapidly in morning sunlight under field conditions.
“Light soaking immediately prior to measurement is recommended to ensure full recovery,” the researchers said. “In addition, when multiple light-based measurements are conducted on the same sample, the UV dose history should be carefully controlled to maintain consistency.”
The findings are presented in “
Metastable dark degradation and light recovery in UV exposed commercial TOPCon
,” published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells
“These findings show that light-induced metastability operates on the same timescale as the natural day–night cycle of fielded modules and must be considered when assessing long-term degradation mechanisms,” the scientists concluded. “Future studies correlating this effect with detailed material properties – such as layer thickness, composition, and microstructure – as well as fielded module studies, will be critical for understanding and improving the predictive capacity of TOPCon module degradation models.”
The research group was formed by scientists from Case Western Reserve University, University of Central Florida,
Arizona State University
and US-based manufacturer
GAF Energy

title: Flanders to cut subsidies for large solar parks - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Flemish government is reducing the subsidy available to solar park owners during periods of negative price hours. The move is expected to save around €189 million ($206.5 million).
Patrick Jowett
15 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Utility-scale
The government in the Belgian region of Flanders is cutting back on subsidies for large solar parks.
Flanders’ Energy Minister Melissa Depraetere is lowering green power certificates for corporate solar parks. Under current rules, solar park owners can receive subsidy payments during periods of negative prices for up to six hours at a time.
The Flemish government is lowering this threshold to fifteen minutes, with European regulations preventing the complete abolition of the subsidy. The change also applies to owners of wind power plants in the region.
“Families with solar panels pay to feed electricity into the grid, while large installations receive subsidies even during periods of oversupply. That is difficult to explain,” Depraetere said.
The minister says the change will save €179 million ($206.5 million) from electricity bills. Reports from Flanders estimates this will translate into an annual saving for households of around €6.
We are putting an end to over-subsidization and thereby removing unnecessary costs from the electricity bill. As a result, the electricity bill will decrease for all Flemish families, and we are making the system fairer,” Depraetere added.
The reduction is also seen as an attempt to curb the frequency of negative hours, by incentivising solar park owners to implement battery storage or halt production during peak hours.
The measure forms part of a broader shift in energy tax across Flanders. Analysis published by Depraetere’s social democratic party Vooruit says the minister’s cabinet is working toward saving the average Flemish household around €80 a year on energy bills from 2028, increasing to nearly €150 a year if the household has installed a heat pump.
Flanders is Belgium’s largest solar market. According to analysis from the International Energy Agency Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme (IEA-PVPS), the region installed an estimated 800 MW of solar last year, taking cumulative capacity past 7 GW.

title: Rheem launches air-to-water heat pumps for multifamily houses - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Rheem’s Torin commercial air-to-water heat pumps achieve a COP of up to 4.5. The units can also deliver outlet-water temperatures of up to 65.6 C.
Emiliano Bellini
15 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The 20 kW system
US-based heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration (HVACR) and water heating products provider
has introduced its Torin commercial heat pump for domestic hot water and hydronic space-heating applications.
The new products are available in 20 kW and 35 kW versions and use R-454B refrigerant.
The two models have nominal heating capacities of 68,000 BTU/h (20 kW) and 120,000 BTU/h (35 kW). Both units operate on a 480 V, three-phase, 60 Hz electrical supply and are intended for indoor or outdoor installation.
The heat pumps rely on inverter-driven compressors. Rheem lists a coefficient of performance (COP) of 4.5 under US Department of Energy (DOE) test conditions, based on an ambient temperature of 26.7 C, an inlet-water temperature of 21.1 C and an outlet-water temperature of 48.9 C.
The manufacturer said the units can operate at outdoor temperatures as low as -25 C and deliver water at temperatures of up to 65.6 C. They support single-pass and multipass hydraulic configurations.
The 20 kW model measures approximately 1,016 mm × 1,016 mm × 1,067 mm and weighs 163 kg. It has a rated power input of 4.9 kW and supports water flow rates of between 18.9 liters/min and 56.8 liters/min.
The 35 kW version measures 1,016 mm × 1,016 mm × 1,473 mm and weighs about 219 kg. Its rated input is 9.8 kW, with supported flow rates ranging from 18.9 liters/min to 75.7 liters/min.
Both models use a double-wall, 316L stainless-steel water heat exchanger and 25.4 mm copper water connections. Their stated sound level is 75 dB(A) at a distance of 3.05 meters.
Up to 16 units can be installed in a cascade arrangement to provide additional capacity or redundancy. The systems include Rheem’s Sky-35 touchscreen controller and support integration with building-management systems through BACnet and Modbus interfaces.
The heat pumps are Energy Star certified and carry NSF/ANSI 5, 61 and 372 certifications.
With the new product line, Rheem is targeting hotels, multifamily buildings, educational campuses, offices and government facilities.

title: CATL launches 170 Wh/kg battery platform for heavy-duty transport with 621-mile range
content: Diesel long dictated the roads, but electric heavy transport is taking charge. CATL unveiled its next-generation modular commercial vehicle battery platform, TECTRANS II, at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover. Rather than a basic cell update, the system is a adaptable modular architecture that integrates into existing vehicle lines. Truck manufacturers can achieve up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles) of range on a single charge, backed by megawatt-level fast charging that replenishes 80% capacity in 25 minutes. CATL rates the heavy-duty truck setup for a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometer operating lifecycle while retaining 70 percent capacity. “Commercial vehicle electrification is emerging as the third wave of the global energy transition,” said Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business. “Across products, energy, services and ecosystem, CATL is poised to work with partners around the world to catch this third wave.” 12 years of fleet duty Diesel engines offered endless range, rapid refueling, and standard parts that kept maintenance cheap. On the other hand, battery electric alternatives meant heavy, expensive packs that ate into cargo limits and spent hours anchored to slow chargers. That might finally be solved, thanks to CATL. TECTRANS II aims to simplify heavy vehicle electrification across diverse fleet operations. Its flexible modular design accommodates up to 1,000 kilometers of range and adapts easily to both charging and battery swapping. Manufacturers can standardize their chassis designs while upgrading battery chemistry over time. Notably, standardized components will help developers to cut vehicle design timelines in half and slash early development costs. As a result, commercial fleets lower upfront investments and maximize operational returns throughout the vehicle lifecycle. TECTRANS II boosts commercial vehicle profitability through lower upfront costs and higher daily operating returns. The battery delivers a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, exceeding the industry average by 13% and increasing payload capacity by 0.6 tonnes. Maximum configurations support megawatt fast charging to hit 80 percent capacity in 25 minutes. Interestingly, a full-tab low-impedance design drives system round-trip efficiency up to 96 percent to limit energy waste. Ultra-durable TECTRANS II Durability, however, is where CATL hopes to truly bury diesel. Fleet managers don’t care about sleek aesthetics, but more about uptime and resale value. To prove the battery can handle harsh things, CATL designed a hot-formed steel cover capable of taking 10,000 steps from an 180-kilogram adult without deforming, paired with an armored bottom plate that withstands 1,000 Joules of road-debris impact. Inside it, independent multi-branch management systems mean that if a single battery line suffers a fault, it isolates automatically. And the rest of the pack continues delivering power, avoiding tow trucks and stranded cargo. It also comes with standard 15-year corrosion resistance that protects units against harsh coastal and winter road conditions. CATL signed a Memorandum of Understanding with DHL Group to establish Green Freight Corridors across Europe, building on their prior late-2024 partnership. Combining DHL’s extensive logistics network with CATL’s battery technology, the companies will collaborate with vehicle manufacturers to design purpose-built electric trucks and launch pilot deployments along key transit routes. “Commercial vehicle electrification will unfold over more than a decade,” said Zhu Lingbo, CTO of CATL Global Business Unit. With megawatt charging, standard modularity, and heavy haulage range finally in place, that decade-long shift looks less like a distant goal and more like an active rollout.

title: US firm unveils new 72-foot drone with 10,357-mile range to replace aging Reaper fleet
content: Swarm Aero has unveiled a new long-range uncrewed aircraft designed to compete for the U.S. Air Force’s planned replacement for the MQ-9A Reaper. The company revealed its Gamera aircraft on the opening day of the Air, Space and Cyber conference, presenting a full-scale model of a drone built around long endurance, modular payloads, and swarm operations. The California-based startup says Gamera will have a 72-foot wingspan and an unrefueled range of up to 9,000 nautical miles (about 10,357 miles). The aircraft is being developed for the Pentagon’s Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA) program, which seeks a lower-cost and more attrition-tolerant aircraft for long-range intelligence and strike missions. Twin-fuselage design sets Gamera apart Gamera uses two parallel fuselages instead of the central fuselage found on the MQ-9A . The layout resembles the twin-boom configuration used by Israel Aerospace Industries’ Heron TP, while its connecting tail structure also recalls the North American Rockwell OV-10 Bronco. A major difference is the engine position. Gamera places a Honeywell TPE331 turboprop in a nacelle mounted between the two fuselages above the wing. Its propeller uses a tractor configuration, with the propeller positioned ahead of the engine. The unusual arrangement also affects the landing gear. Gamera uses four landing-gear assemblies positioned inside the two fuselages, allowing weapons to be carried beneath the center section without interfering with the nose gear. Built for range and modular payloads Swarm says Gamera will have seven hardpoints for weapons and other mission equipment. The MMA program calls for an aircraft capable of carrying at least 2,800 pounds of payload, including weapons such as the AGM-158C Long Range Anti-Ship Missile. The aircraft is being designed with modular hardware and avionics so payloads and systems can be changed as missions evolve. Its range and payload can also be adjusted according to mission requirements. Swarm has been developing Gamera since 2022 and has worked on manufacturing methods intended to support high-volume production. The company says automated composite manufacturing and modular avionics could help reduce production costs. One operator could control 35 drones Swarm is also building Gamera around autonomous swarm operations. Its control architecture is designed to allow one operator to manage as many as 35 aircraft simultaneously. The company has developed its own autonomy system, called Legion, and was selected for a Defense Innovation Unit effort focused on command and control for drone swarms under the Replicator initiative. The approach aims is make large numbers of long-range aircraft practical to operate. Swarm has also received Air Force Research Laboratory funding for manufacturing and large-UAS development. Gamera enters Reaper replacement race The MMA program is seeking an aircraft priced far below the MQ-9A, which can cost up to $50 million depending on configuration. Air Force officials have set a target of about $10 million per aircraft and are accelerating efforts to field the new system. Swarm will face competition from established defense companies. General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, which produces the MQ-9 family, has already revealed its own MMA candidate, called Wildfire. The firm plans to fly the first Gamera later next year. The company also sees potential civilian uses for the aircraft, including logistics and firefighting, although the U.S. military remains its primary target market.

title: USAF to field 500 collaborative combat aircraft by 2032, named GA FQ-42 and FQ-4
content: The U.S. Air Force plans to field at least 500 Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) by 2032, sharply expanding its ambitions for semi-autonomous aircraft that can fight alongside human pilots. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink announced the target on September 14 while revealing the official names of the service’s first two CCAs: General Atomics’ FQ-42 Vengeance and Anduril’s FQ-44 Fury. The aircraft are designed to work alongside crewed fighters such as the F-35 and future F-47, providing additional sensors, weapons and other capabilities without putting another pilot in each aircraft. Air Force wants hundreds of robotic wingmen The new target represents a significant increase from the Air Force’s previous plans. In June, the service said it intended to procure more than 150 combat-capable CCAs by the end of the decade after awarding production contracts to General Atomics and Anduril. The service now wants at least 500 in operation by 2032. The Air Force has separately described an overall goal of approximately 1,000 combat-capable CCAs, with the program built around continued competition and successive increments. The FQ-42 and FQ-44 are the first Increment 1 aircraft. Their job is not to replace conventional fighters but to increase what a crewed aircraft can do by distributing sensing, weapons, and other functions across a larger formation. Rather than remotely flying each aircraft throughout a mission, the CCA concept relies on semi-autonomous systems that can handle navigation and other tasks within parameters established by human operators. According to Army Recognition ,  The Air Force has already moved the aircraft beyond basic flight testing. In July, a YFQ-44A fired an AIM-120 air-to-air missile at a digital target during a live-fire test. The service stressed that humans retain control of weapon employment and that CCAs will not autonomously decide to fire. The aircraft have also been tested in more realistic operating conditions. During an Agile Combat Employment exercise at Creech Air Force Base in Nevada, the Air Force generated multiple CCA sorties, integrated the unmanned aircraft with crewed platforms and evaluated operations from a dispersed location. Software will be as important as the aircraft The Air Force is also separating CCA mission-autonomy software from the aircraft themselves. Its government-owned Autonomy Government Reference Architecture is intended to allow software from different suppliers to be integrated across compatible platforms. Six companies, including Anduril, General Atomics , Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, RTX Collins Aerospace and Shield AI, are competing to develop mission-autonomy software for the program. The approach is intended to keep competition alive and allow the Air Force to introduce improved autonomy without redesigning the aircraft. The scale of the new target, however, presents a major production and operational challenge. The Air Force will need to manufacture hundreds of aircraft while developing the maintenance, weapons, communications, and command-and-control infrastructure needed to operate them. For General Atomics and Anduril, the transition is already underway. The FQ-42 Vengeance and FQ-44 Fury have moved from prototype designations into production, while the Air Force continues testing how humans and autonomous aircraft can work together. If the service reaches 500 aircraft by 2032, CCAs will no longer be an experimental addition to American airpower . They will represent a substantial new layer of the U.S. fighter force. One designed to put more aircraft, sensors, and weapons into contested airspace without requiring a corresponding increase in pilots.

title: Nearly 1,000 small nuclear reactors could exist by 2060, output to top 1,284 GWe: IAEA
content: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has increased its long-term nuclear power forecast for the sixth year in a row. In its latest projections, shared at the 70th General Conference in Vienna, the agency says global nuclear capacity could reach 1,284 GWe by 2060 if the most optimistic scenario plays out. This growth could involve building hundreds of small modular reactors (SMRs). The report, Energy, Electricity and Nuclear Power Estimates for the Period up to 2060, is the first time the IAEA has projected nuclear capacity out to 2060. In the high-case scenario, global nuclear capacity would be 3.4 times higher than it was at the end of 2025. Nuclear capacity set for long-term growth By the end of 2025, there were 413 nuclear reactors running around the world, generating 377.1 GWe of electricity. The IAEA now predicts that capacity could reach 1,045 GWe by 2050 in its high-case scenario, which is higher than its previous estimate of 992 GWe. By 2060, nuclear capacity could rise to 1,284 GWe. The low-case scenario is more cautious, predicting 641 GWe by 2050 and 696 GWe by 2060. Previously, the low-case forecast for 2050 was 561 GWe. These projections consider current reactors, possible license renewals, planned shutdowns, and construction projects that are likely in the next few decades. The high-case scenario assumes countries will make bigger commitments to nuclear energy, while the low-case scenario expects current trends to continue with few policy changes. “The IAEA projections show the increasing role of nuclear power in meeting the world’s growing electricity needs. To realize this potential, investment in new nuclear capacity and reactor lifetime extensions will be essential,” stated IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi. SMRs could add hundreds of reactors SMRs are expected to play a big role in this growth. The IAEA defines an SMR as a reactor with up to 300 MWe of capacity, and there are currently more than 100 designs in development. In the high-case scenario, SMRs could make up 28 percent of the 1,017 GWe of new nuclear capacity added by 2060, or about 284 GWe. If each SMR averages 300 MWe, that would mean about 946 reactors. If the average is 250 MWe, it would be around 1,136 reactors. SMRs could also play a big role in certain regions. In North America, about 60% of new nuclear capacity could come from SMRs. The IAEA expects a 40 percent share in both South-Eastern Asia and Latin America and the Caribbean. Older reactors remain important Extending the life of current reactors will also affect future capacity. Under the high case, about 70 percent of today’s operating nuclear capacity could remain online in 2060. The low case assumes almost two-thirds of current reactors are expected to retire. The IAEA says that “a lifetime extension for an existing reactor, if it is viable, is one of the most cost-effective baseload low-emission electricity sources and is of particular importance for regions with aging nuclear fleets.” Financing is another key factor. The agency notes that since energy crises began in 2022, concerns about energy security and interest in more diverse electricity sources have shifted focus to nuclear power. Nuclear demand grows despite changing share Global nuclear electricity generation went up by 1 percent in 2025 compared to 2024. But since total global electricity generation grew by 2.7 percent, nuclear’s share dropped from 8.7 percent to 8.4 percent. The IAEA said, “The upward revision of the projections reflects growing recognition of the role that nuclear power can play in supporting energy security and long-term economic growth. There has been renewed engagement with nuclear power by international financial institutions, such as the World Bank Group and the Asian Development Bank, signaling a broader shift that other international financial institutions have begun to follow. “Energy security and affordability concerns intensified following successive energy crises since 2022. Disruptions to oil and gas flows have major implications for both energy security and global energy markets. In response, interest in diversified electricity generation has grown, including interest in nuclear power.” The World Nuclear Association is even more optimistic, estimating that global nuclear capacity could reach 1,457 GWe by 2050 if countries meet their targets and current reactors keep running.

title: BYD unveils 373-mile range electric truck that charges in 20 minutes
content: Chinese automaker BYD has unveiled its advanced electric commercial vehicle lineup for Europe at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hannover, Germany. The portfolio houses a heavy-duty tractor offering up to 373 miles of range and 1.5-megawatt charging.Presented on September 14 at IAA, the portfolio addresses urban distribution, municipal work, regional transport, and long-haul logistics.IAA is an international trade fair organized every two years by the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA). It serves as a platform for the commercial vehicles, logistics, and transport sectors.BYD is combining its vehicles with batteries, charging infrastructure, energy storage, energy management, and financial services to support fleet electrification through a single ecosystem.Heavy truck charges in about 20 minutesThe flagship is a 4×2 electric tractor, named ETT 44, designed for combinations weighing up to 48.5 tons. Developed from the ground up as a dedicated electric platform, it uses a 651-kWh Blade Battery operating on an 851-volt architecture.Its powertrain produces around 733 horsepower under rated conditions and approximately 986 horsepower at peak output. BYD claims the truck can cover up to 373 miles on a single charge, positioning it for regional and long-haul freight operations.A standard CCS2 DC charger provides up to 420 kW, taking the battery from 20 percent to 80 percent in about an hour. BYD’s Megawatt Charging System raises charging power beyond 1.5 MW and cuts the same charging session to roughly 20 minutes.“We have already put FLASH Charging into practice in passenger vehicles. Today, we are bringing this technology to commercial vehicles, starting with our trucks. With 1.5 Megawatts of charging power, it can charge from 20% to 80% in about 20 minutes – delivering up to 248 miles of range. Less time charging. More time on the road,” said Stella Li, Executive Vice President of BYD.Extended warranty supports fleet operatorsBYD is backing the truck’s Blade Battery with a standard warranty of 10 years or approximately 746,000 miles. The company says this goes beyond the base-vehicle and battery warranties typically offered in Europe, where extended coverage is usually a paid option.The heavy-duty model also features a driver-focused cabin and multiple assistance and safety technologies. Adaptive cruise control, autonomous emergency braking, lane-keeping assistance, and blind-spot detection are included as standard.Beyond the flagship tractor, BYD displayed 4×2 and 6×2 rigid trucks, including swap-body and hooklift versions, alongside the E-Vali light commercial van and EYT 2.0 electric yard tractor. The portfolio spans approximately 3.9 to 48.5 tons, covering work from city deliveries to distribution-yard and heavy road operations.One ecosystem for fleet electrificationBYD presented the lineup through its Total Cost of Mobility philosophy, which treats the vehicle, energy consumption, electricity pricing, charging infrastructure, operations, lifecycle management, and financing as parts of one system.Its vertically integrated approach brings vehicle development, Blade Batteries, megawatt chargers, energy storage, and energy management together. BYD revealed the model can reduce operational complexity, improve uptime, and accelerate the path toward profitable electric fleets.BYD’s commercial vehicles currently operate in more than 100 countries and over 400 cities. With its expanded European portfolio, the company is positioning itself as a single provider of electric commercial vehicles and the energy infrastructure needed to operate them.

title: US deploys first on-orbit weapon as China warns of space arms race
content: The U.S. has publicly disclosed that it deployed an “on-orbit” space weapon for the first time. Reportedly, the nation has framed it as a necessary step to counter growing counterspace threats from Russia and China, while Beijing has warned against inciting a space arms race.At an Air Force conference in Maryland, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink carefully announced the explosive news to warn potential rivals.After the announcement, China urged the United States to stop expanding its outer-space military and to stop preparing for war, warning that such moves risk triggering an orbital arms race. “Today we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink stated at the conference. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”He refused to provide details. He would not say when the hardware was launched, how many systems circle the globe, or precisely what they do. The message, however, was clear. The cosmos is no longer just for reconnaissance and GPS, but it could become an active battlefield. Orbital standoffCiting Chinese and Russian efforts to target American satellites in potential future conflicts, senior US military leaders previously signaled plans to strengthen their orbital defense posture. Washington has now confirmed the existence of its space weapon, but the officials have kept all operational details strictly classified.“Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary,” BBC quoted a U.S. Space Force spokesperson. “These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes at the direction of combatant commands.”While the 1967 Outer Space Treaty strictly bans weapons of mass destruction in Earth’s orbit, it leaves a wide opening for conventional military hardware.Defense analyst Dr. Bleddyn Bowen of the Royal United Services Institute told the BBC that very little public information exists regarding the deployed technology, which could encompass several distinct weapon systems. He speculated that the asset is most likely an orbital electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, similar to terrestrial technology used to block communications. A kinetic kill vehicle that physically impacts and destroys satellites remains a possibility; however, this scenario is far less plausible because it would produce a dangerous volume of space debris.Growing threat Yet, the rapid reveal coincides with accelerated momentum behind the administration’s “Golden Dome” missile defense framework, which includes space-based interceptors. Beijing reacted almost immediately. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urged Washington to stop expanding its military footprint off the planet, warning against a catastrophic space arms race. Washington counters that it had no choice. Revelations from early February indicate that two Russian satellites likely intercepted signals from at least twelve European spacecraft following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Experts warn that these interceptions could have allowed Russian intelligence services to read sensitive transmitted data or potentially take direct control of the satellites.This follows a 2024 U.S. warning regarding a separate Russian satellite launch believed to possess offensive counterspace capabilities, an allegation Moscow has not publicly addressed.“China develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy,” the U.S. Space Force’s website noted.  On the other hand, “Russia views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts.”By stepping through that legal opening so publicly, the U.S. has officially fired the starting gun on a new era of orbital brinkmanship.

title: World-first: 17-tower system to extract rare metals from lithium waste
content: China secured supply chain dominance and established rubidium as a strategic resource by extracting high-value elements from its lithium waste.Institute of Process Engineering (CAS), alongside Ganfeng Lithium, has launched the world’s first 500-tonne annual capacity production line in Jiangxi province to extract rubidium and cesium from lithium mining waste.The institute successfully deployed a 17-tower industrial extraction unit that ran smoothly from its initial launch. Both end products, cesium carbonate and rubidium carbonate, emerge at over 99.9 percent purity and are already being sold in commercial batches.Rubidium and cesium are highly important rare metals for tech. These rare metals anchor the advanced hardware like atomic clocks, aerospace navigation, biomedical research, solid-state batteries, and quantum computing networks.Squeezing rare metals from slagRubidium and cesium rarely exist in large amounts as independent minerals in the Earth’s crust. These elements hide in low concentrations inside lithium ores and salt-lake brines. Miners struggle to recover them because their low grades complicate standard chemical extraction. The complex chemical bonds make separation costly and difficult. Eventually, the firms dumped the valuable slag into waste piles and wrote off the metals inside.But not anymore, with this new method that uses a 17-tower extraction system and no roasting tanks. The new design uses 17 extraction columns across four core processing sections to handle tasks that previously required over 70 conventional tanks. One column delivers the separation efficiency of up to 15 regular stages. This setup slashes solvent consumption by 40 percent and cuts the equipment footprint by more than half. As a result, the streamlined facility runs continuously and is fully automated, with significantly lower resource needs.It works through differential counter-current extraction. The South China Morning Post reported that the line recovers more than 98 percent of the available cesium and over 95 percent of the rubidium. Cutting overseas dependencyChina possesses extensive rubidium and cesium reserves locked inside specialty lithium ores and salt-lake brines. An earlier study pointed to domestic reserves of 1.16 million tonnes of rubidium oxide and 140,000 tonnes of cesium oxide. From a strategic perspective, this development resolves a major vulnerability in domestic supply chains. Although China possesses nearly 40 percent of global rubidium reserves embedded in lepidolite deposits, it lacks commercially viable pollucite reserves for cesium. Beijing has mostly imported raw cesium ore from Canada, Australia, and Zimbabwe.But now, China can insulate its high-tech sector through the recovery of both metals from domestic industrial runoff. Combined with existing operations, the country now commands a domestic capacity of roughly 3,000 tonnes of rubidium salt equivalent per year.This strategy replicates China’s long-standing approach to rare earths: combining massive domestic mineral processing with proprietary extraction technology to drive production costs well below those of foreign competitors.As next-generation tech like perovskite solar cells and quantum networks scale up, demand for these niche metals will explode.The demonstration line shows that low-grade, associated rubidium and cesium resources can be processed industrially through clean, high-efficiency extraction. This achievement validates a scalable technical design for broader commercial expansion across the industry.

title: Tiny autonomous boat completes historic 3,555-mile Atlantic crossing
content: A four-foot autonomous sailboat has completed a 3,555-mile Atlantic crossing, becoming the first vessel to win the long-running Microtransat Challenge after more than 30 previous attempts.The Oshen C-Star PC13 departed Gran Canaria on May 7 and reached Barbados 127 days later. During the voyage, the tiny uncrewed vessel had to navigate busy shipping routes, changing weather, and waves reaching around 30 feet, including conditions associated with Tropical Storm Dolly.The achievement marks the first successful completion of the Microtransat, an autonomous sailing challenge established in 2010 to push the development of robotic boats. The competition’s rules require vessels to cross the Atlantic without outside assistance or human intervention in their decision-making once they are underway.A tiny boat with a long-distance missionThe PC13 is designed around a deceptively simple idea: let the wind provide most of the propulsion while software handles navigation.Before departure, the boat’s waypoints were programmed into its onboard computer. From there, its autonomous navigation system determined how to reach them by continuously assessing conditions, including wind direction and speed, currents, and available battery power.The boat has a solar-powered thruster that can help it maneuver in light winds, but Microtransat rules prohibited its use during the crossing. That left the PC13 largely dependent on its sail and its ability to make good navigation decisions.According to reports, the journey was Oshen’s third attempt. Its 2023 attempt ended after about 20 days and just 6.2 miles. A second attempt in 2024 lasted 277 days and reached roughly three-quarters of the way across the Atlantic before heavy seas destroyed the sail.Those failures helped the company refine the design for longer deployments. During this year’s crossing, the PC13 developed erratic steering around the halfway point, which Oshen believes may have been caused by excessive friction in the rudder. The vessel eventually corrected itself and continued toward the Caribbean.From racing robot to ocean sensorThe crossing is ultimately a demonstration of endurance rather than speed. Oshen’s C-Star vessels are intended primarily as autonomous sensor platforms that can operate in places where deploying and maintaining conventional monitoring equipment is difficult.The boats can collect measurements including sea-surface temperature, air temperature, atmospheric pressure, humidity, salinity and water density. That could make fleets of relatively inexpensive autonomous vessels useful for building persistent datasets across parts of the ocean that are poorly monitored today.Oshen has already demonstrated the concept in extreme conditions. In 2025, one of its C-Stars was deployed into Hurricane Humberto near the U.S. Virgin Islands for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and survived for hours inside the storm’s eyewall while transmitting environmental data.The company now wants to scale from individual vessels to autonomous constellations. It says C-Stars are already being used in the Caribbean for hurricane monitoring and that it plans a larger fleet for North Atlantic climate monitoring.That approach could eventually turn autonomous boats into something resembling a distributed network of floating weather stations, gathering measurements continuously without requiring a crewed vessel to remain at sea.The same endurance could have applications beyond environmental science. Oshen has said future C-Stars could carry hydrophones to listen for underwater activity. At the same time, their autonomous operation and ability to remain at sea could help monitor illegal fishing or vessels attempting to operate without transmitting their positions.The Microtransat achievement represents more than a tiny boat completing a very long journey. It shows that autonomous surface vessels can now combine renewable propulsion, onboard sensing, and navigation software to operate independently for months at a time.For ocean researchers, that could mean more persistent data. For maritime operators, it could eventually mean a much larger network of small robotic vessels watching over parts of the ocean that remain difficult and expensive to monitor.

title: U.S. firms join forces to upscale hypersonic manufacturing base
content: VulcanForms and Specter Aerospace are partnering to build a dedicated U.S. manufacturing operation for airbreathing hypersonic weapons, targeting one of the biggest challenges facing the technology. Producing systems at scale.The companies said the partnership will combine Specter’s experience developing hypersonic vehicles with VulcanForms’ high-volume metal additive manufacturing and post-processing capabilities. The goal is to move hypersonic systems beyond development and testing toward more scalable production of munitions, interceptors and cruise missiles.Building a production pipeline for hypersonicsThe partnership was announced by the two companies as demand grows for hypersonic weapons and other high-speed systems. Specter says it has worked with the Department of Defense since its founding in 2013 and is developing long-range hypersonic technology for U.S. forces and allies.The companies said they are already using production-ready facilities operated by both organizations while evaluating locations for a future dedicated manufacturing facility. They are conducting a nationwide site evaluation, but have not disclosed where the facility would be located, how much it will cost, or how much production capacity it will eventually provide.The planned operation is intended to cover more than just individual components. The companies said it will support manufacturing and end-to-end integration, meaning the effort is intended to bring together the manufacturing and assembly processes needed to produce complete weapon systems rather than simply supplying individual printed parts.That distinction is important for hypersonic weapons, where complex propulsion, thermal-management, and aerodynamic components must work together under extreme conditions.VulcanForms specializes in digitally driven metal additive manufacturing alongside machining, inspection and other production processes. Its aerospace operations work with materials including titanium and nickel-based superalloys and are designed to produce flight-critical components for aerospace applications.The company says its manufacturing platform can handle production ranging from prototypes and pilot runs to high-volume manufacturing, with facilities in Devens and Newburyport, Massachusetts.Why manufacturing is becoming a hypersonic bottleneckHypersonic weapons are difficult to manufacture not simply because they fly extremely fast, but because their propulsion and structures have to survive severe thermal and mechanical environments.Airbreathing systems such as ramjets and scramjets must also manage airflow and combustion at extreme speeds. Components can require complex internal geometries, specialized materials, and tight manufacturing tolerances.Additive manufacturing can be useful in this environment because it allows engineers to produce geometries that can be difficult or expensive to manufacture using conventional methods.Specter has already been using additive manufacturing and computational design to shorten its development cycles. In a separate collaboration with software company nTop, Specter said it reduced the iteration time for one regeneratively cooled engine configuration from more than a day to less than 20 minutes. The company has also demonstrated a workflow for generating and analyzing multiple hypersonic vehicle configurations from parametric models.The new partnership attempts to carry that philosophy into production. Specter has also been pursuing other lower-cost high-speed systems. In February, it announced a collaboration with Sierra Nevada Corporation on a supersonic aerial-effects product line using Specter’s ramjet and scramjet propulsion expertise. The companies said they were targeting scalable manufacturing and affordability, with initial flight testing scheduled for the third quarter of 2026.For VulcanForms, the partnership extends its existing focus on building domestic manufacturing capacity for high-performance industries. The company has argued that integrating additive manufacturing, machining, inspection, and digital production workflows can shorten lead times while strengthening U.S. supply chains.If the partnership succeeds, its significance could extend beyond one weapon program. The objective is to create a manufacturing base that can produce airbreathing hypersonic systems at a higher cadence and lower cost than traditional production methods have allowed. For the U.S. hypersonics effort, that could be just as important as developing another vehicle capable of flying at extreme speeds.

title: CERN scientists spot quantum entanglement between a pair of Z bosons
content: Scientists at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have spotted spooky quantum entanglement in Z bosons, particles produced from a Higgs boson, for the first time. This isn’t the first time quantum entanglement has been observed in particles generated at the LHC, but it is surely in a different set of particles, and one that also has a virtual counterpart. Quantum entanglement is a phenomenon observed in quantum physics that even stumped the great Albert Einstein. Two particles are said to be quantum entangled when their properties are so closely linked that the state of one is dependent on the state of the other. This holds even when the two particles are separated by a large distance from each other, prompting Einstein to call this behavior ‘spooky’. Even though we do not completely understand this, we have been able to leverage it to build technologies like quantum computing and communications. These might still be in their infancy but promise a brand new tomorrow that will be drastically different from the present. How little we know about this behavior is evident in the fact that scientists at the CERN are still making new discoveries about them. Quantum entanglement in Z bosonsThe ATLAS experiment at CERN first detected quantum entanglement in a pair of top quarks produced by the LHC in 2024. The recent discovery of quantum entanglement in Z bosons is a bit different because, unlike top quarks, Z bosons have three spin states, also known as qutrits. Z bosons are produced briefly at the LHC when a Higgs boson splits in its journey of further decay. However, since a Higgs boson does not have a spin of its own, the two Z bosons formed during its decay cannot have any odd combinations of spins. Their spins cancel each other out, resulting in the zero spin for the Higgs boson. It is likely that the two Z bosons have a shared state that makes this possible. However, there is a major issue in their production. A Higgs boson has a mass of 125 GeV, while Z bosons weigh 91 GeV. This makes it impossible for a Higgs boson to produce two Z bosons at once, which leaves only one option: one of the Z bosons is virtual. Quantum entanglement gets spookierEven as quantum physicists regularly deal with spooky particle behavior, virtual particles are a strange phenomenon for them to deal with as well. These particles emerge during particle collisions but can’t be observed like other particles. So, the question was whether they can actually participate in entanglement. Confirming this scientifically was even tougher, since Z bosons themselves last for 3 x 10-25 seconds. So, even the real boson is barely available to measure its spin. So how could scientists confirm the spin of its virtual counterpart? The researchers turned to clues available from the decay of Z bosons. The decay of each Z boson produces two charged particles, either leptons or muons, giving potentially four particles that can be detected. The direction of travel of these particles gives scientists information they can use to work backward and determine the spins of the bosons that created them. While this sounds simple, the research team at CERN had a hard time finding sufficient data to study it. Even after sifting through years of particle collision data, they could only find 400 events where Z bosons split into four leptons. The data showed a preference for an entangled state over a non-entangled state with a sigma, or statistical significance, of 4.7, close to the number five that scientists prefer to achieve before making a major claim. There is more work to be done in this area and much to be discovered about the virtual particles and how they behave. The results were published in Physical Review Letters.

title: Lockheed's stealth drone with 38-foot wingspan set to fly by 2027
content: Lockheed Martin is expanding its Vectis stealth drone program by developing four additional prototypes alongside the aircraft already in production. The company announced the investment at the Association of the Air and Space Forces conference in National Harbor, Maryland.The new aircraft will help Lockheed accelerate flight testing and validate how Vectis can be manufactured quickly and affordably. The prototype, announced in 2025, is expected to make its maiden flight by the end of 2027.“Development work on those additional aircraft is already underway, and we’ll have more specifics to share soon,” said Ron Fehlen, head of Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works advanced development division.Stealth drone built to team with fightersLockheed describes Vectis as a large Group 5 stealth drone designed to support several mission types. Depending on customer requirements, the unmanned aircraft could be configured for air-to-air combat, air-to-ground operations, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions.Although Fehlen did not name potential customers, he said Vectis is more closely aligned with Collaborative Combat Aircraft programs than the Mass Modular Aircraft initiative. Collaborative Combat Aircraft are intended to operate alongside crewed fighter jets.“There is no reason to say, Well, it’s one customer or another,” he said.Vectis is approximately 34 feet long and has a wingspan of about 38 feet. That makes the tailless aircraft roughly as long as an MQ-9 Reaper, while its wingspan is comparable to that of an F-35 fighter jet.Lockheed is also aiming to offer the aircraft at a cost that can compete within the Collaborative Combat Aircraft market. Fehlen said the company is targeting unit costs “to be [at] the CCA competitive price.”Top-mounted inlet supports austere operationsOne of Vectis’ notable design features is a submerged air inlet positioned on top of its airframe. According to Fehlen, the placement helps reduce aerodynamic drag while limiting the risk of debris entering the aircraft.That protection could simplify maintenance when the drone operates from austere locations, where runways and surrounding environments may contain material that could damage an engine.The company displayed a full-scale model of Vectis at the conference and released new images showing the first prototype being assembled. Lockheed has not disclosed how much it is investing in the program.Ikea-like assembly cuts labor requirementsSkunk Works is using a manufacturing method called minimal tooling determinate assembly to simplify production and reduce costs. Fehlen compared the approach to assembling furniture from Ikea because it allows parts to be joined with less tooling and manual work.“It’s a technique that really enables an increased level of affordability and speed through really reducing the amount of touch labor required and increasing the first pass yield,” he said. “We’ve seen, in many cases, an 80 percent reduction in labor hours to build up the aircraft itself,” he added. Development has also moved rapidly. Fehlen said the team progressed from an initial design to wind-tunnel validation in two months, completed its first digital build in six months, and released the first component for production in eight months.
